body:
I am also checking in here because of this. 

So 2 things I found

1. it seems openai returns function calls in streams https://community.openai.com/t/function-calls-and-streaming/263393/2
2. this SDK uses its AIStream in which the customParser is only looking at delta.content.text so it swallows the possibility to stream the function call response

To your question regarding JSON closing tags, I implemented a month ago a streaming plugin aware chatbot. What you are looking for is basically a parser that whenever you see tokens that technically matches json in its correct syntax, you buffer them, until you have a full valid JSON, and than you yield that whole thing. 

To make it easier, I used prompt engineering to wrap any json into a |START| and |END| tag. This way I can more easily start buffering

So in the end you will have a stream that looks like

Of
course
let
me
check
the 
plugin 
|START| -- start buffering now
.buffer: {
.buffer: { function_call
.buffer: { function_call: check_the_weather, arguments ...}
|END| -- set the model with a stop word to equal |END| 

Anyways that is a completely different implementation than open ai suggests, as the function calls from them cannot come along with text from the AI. But still I thought worth sharing

body:
Update: I have done some testing using the `ai-chatbot` project deployed to Vercel with some logging. Tokens are not generated on the server, in the background, after cancellation.

-----

I am coming to the same conclusion. 

I was very excited to see the release of this library today, particularly this documentation https://sdk.vercel.ai/docs/concepts/backpressure-and-cancellation.

Last month I was asked to add cancellation to a product I am working on for a client. I attempted to get this working with edge functions but could not receive the cancel callback on the server. I decided to see if I could get it working at all and was able to implement a version using Deno since it has a similar runtime API.

At this point, I sent a support request to Vercel and about two weeks later it was confirmed the upstream provider, Cloudflare or AWS, I assume, did not support the abort signal and was aware of this limitation.

I moved our Open AI streaming endpoints to a Fastify server running Node 20 on an AWS ECS cluster. This setup has allowed me to handle the cancellations properly. I can cancel my request to OpenAI, which saves me tokens and writes whatever tokens were received to the db with a "cancel" type.

I did not expect the edge function to receive the AbortController signal, even though the examples use this as the cancellation mechanism. The example of using the `pull` callback in a ReadableStream was something I hadn't tried previously, so I decided to apply the approach to our codebase.

I found that the AIStream doesn't use the `pull` callback but instead has a TransformStream. I looked for `pull` and found it in the Hugging Face example. I converted my `request.body` to an iterator using a similar approach. This also doesn't seem to handle the cancellation. 

I am using the pages directory in our app, assuming that the examples only use the new app directory to highlight it rather than it being a requirement.

> Anything special devs need to do for using cancellation?

The Next.js team hasn't released a new version yet (I'll ping them to see if they can do a canary release), but once they have users just need to `npm install next@latest` (or `next@canary`).

> And what is back-pressure and what do we need to accomodate it?

Back-pressure is explained in https://sdk.vercel.ai/docs/concepts/backpressure-and-cancellation. Essentially, it's the ability for the server pause the stream because the client doesn't need more information yet. Next.js hasn't added support for it yet, but when they do, everyone will need to update their `next` dependency again.

body:
> @jvandenaardweg Same here. Any resolution yet?

Unfortunately no. Just 2 possible workarounds I can think of:

1. When a user initiates a cancel from your UI, send the AI generated text to an API that tracks the token/character/word usage of that text. Probable downside is when a user navigates away from your site (or closes the browser), then the API call will not be fired.

2. Track each generated token using `onToken` on the server and after a certain timeout just assume its cancelled. Also track the completion, so you can cancel them out. But for this you need to keep a record in a Redis store or something. Send each token to that store (that are a lot of requests depending on the size of text being generated). Because once the stream is done, the Edge Function is terminated and your timeout code will not run. Then I guess you need to poll Redis each minute or so and pull that usage info into your main database.

I currently have option 1 in place in my app. Not optimal, but in terms of dev time the easiest I think.

body:
> I've realized using your Langchain interface it's very easy to connect to Azure OpenAI service as shown below. I guess the only remaining question is how to do this with the openai-edge package.
> 
> ```
>   const llm = new ChatOpenAI({
>     streaming: true,
>     callbackManager: CallbackManager.fromHandlers(handlers),
>     azureOpenAIApiVersion: process.env.AZURE_OPENAI_API_VERSION,
>     azureOpenAIApiKey: process.env.AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY,
>     azureOpenAIApiInstanceName: process.env.AZURE_OPENAI_INSTANCE_NAME,
>     azureOpenAIApiDeploymentName:
>       process.env.AZURE_OPENAI_API_DEPLOYMENT_NAME,
>   })
> ```

I think the main issue with the `openai-edge` package is, that it does not provide a way to add query parameters. However, this is required to use the Azure OpenAI endpoints. 

To call an Azure OpenAI endpoint, a consumer must provide the `api-version` query parameter.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cognitive-services/openai/reference

body:
Building off the above answers, here's an example using `experimental_StreamData`:

`server.py`

```python
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

from utils import stream_chunk #formats chunks for use with experimental_StreamData

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

app = FastAPI()

# Added because the frontend and this backend run on separate ports, should change depending on your setup, not a good idea in prod
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
    expose_headers=[ "X-Experimental-Stream-Data"],  # this is needed for streaming data header to be read by the client
)

client = AsyncOpenAI()

@app.post("/ask")
async def ask(req: dict):
    stream = await client.chat.completions.create(
        messages=req["messages"],
        model="gpt-3.5-turbo",
        stream=True,
    )

    async def generator():
        async for chunk in stream:
            yield stream_chunk(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", "text")
        yield stream_chunk([{"foo":"bar"}], "data") # send streaming data after 

    response_messages = generator()
    return StreamingResponse(response_messages, media_type="text/event-stream",  headers={"X-Experimental-Stream-Data": "true"})
```

Where `stream_chunk` is a util that looks like this: 

`utils.py`

```python
# transforms the chunk into a stream part compatible with the vercel/ai
def stream_chunk(chunk, type: str = "text"):
    code = get_stream_part_code(type)
    formatted_stream_part = f"{code}:{json.dumps(chunk, separators=(',', ':'))}\n"
    return formatted_stream_part

# given a type returns the code for the stream part
def get_stream_part_code(stream_part_type: str) -> str:
    stream_part_types = {
        "text": "0",
        "function_call": "1",
        "data": "2",
        "error": "3",
        "assistant_message": "4",
        "assistant_data_stream_part": "5",
        "data_stream_part": "6",
        "message_annotations_stream_part": "7",
    }
    return stream_part_types[stream_part_type]
```

 if chunk.type == "content_block_delta":

to

if chunk.type == "content_block_delta":
    part = '0:{text}\n'.format(text=json.dumps(chunk.delta.text))
    yield part

For some people still struggling with Next.js (useChat) + FastAPI streams - I found that `compress: false` in next.config.js fixes the issue.
It did not satisfy my needs though, as I didn't want to turn of compression for the whole project.
Instead, I set the following headers in my FastAPI StreamingResponse:
```
        response = StreamingResponse(
            stream_text(client_messages),
            media_type="text/plain",
            headers={
                "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
                "Connection": "keep-alive",
                "Content-Encoding": "none",
                "Content-Type": "text/plain",
                "Transfer-Encoding": "chunked",
                "X-Vercel-AI-Data-Stream": "v1"
            },
        )
        return response
```

and the clue was in `"Content-Encoding": "none",`
I know it's not standard, but it's a solution for an issue I've been trying to solve for hours.

hope this helps someone, I wasted too much time on this. Streams work fine now. If no encoding becomes an issue one day, I will come back to it, but for now, I'm glad it works. I did not see a huge response size difference as well.

body:
Hi all,

After some research / asking around, I believe this is a remix issue rather than an SDK one (but please let me know if you disagree!)

Basically Remix uses `node-fetch` and we're using the spec compliant `fetch` implementation. If you use the edge runtime on Vercel it should work:

```
export const config = { runtime: "edge" };
```

You shouldn't need to use the edge runtime though (even though we recommend it) so I'll look into the appropriate way to handle this. It seems like we'll either need to add polyfills to vercel/remix or submit something upstream.

body:
I have a remix app running on vercel, and was running into this issue trying to use the streamText method. What finally ended up working for me is the following:

upgrade node to v20.x previously I was on v18.20.3
I guess the difference here is that in v18 fetch is still experimental
With just the above had my packages at:

      "@vercel/remix": "2.12.0",
      "ai": "3.4.7",
      "@remix-run/node": "^2.10.2",
      "@remix-run/react": "^2.10.2",
      "@remix-run/serve": "^2.10.2"
According to the [remix 2.9.0](https://remix.run/docs/en/main/start/changelog#v290) if you're on node 20.x you need should remove the installGlobals call in `vite.config.js, so I did.

At this point, when running remix vite:dev locally streaming was working but I would run into this TypeError: First parameter has member 'readable' that is not a ReadableStream.  error when deployed to vercel.

**What got it working on a vercel deploy was to provide the undici fetch to the openai provider, like this:**
```
import { fetch } from "undici";
import { createOpenAI } from "@ai-sdk/openai";
import { streamText } from "ai";
....
const openAI = createOpenAI({
      fetch: fetch,
});
const result = await streamText({
     model: openAI('gpt-4o')
     .....
})
....
```
For anyone who is running into this issue, with streamText hope this helps

body:
The first minor change to fix this is definitely updating the docs/demo to use request callback handlers on the `call` as mentioned by https://js.langchain.com/docs/production/callbacks/#when-do-you-want-to-use-each-of-these

```
When do you want to use each of these?
* Constructor callbacks are most useful for use cases such as logging, monitoring, etc., which are not specific to a single request, but rather to the entire chain. For example, if you want to log all the requests made to an LLMChain, you would pass a handler to the constructor.
* Request callbacks are most useful for use cases such as streaming, where you want to stream the output of a single request to a specific websocket connection, or other similar use cases. For example, if you want to stream the output of a single request to a websocket, you would pass a handler to the call() method
```

body:
This is a limitation of the ConversationalRetrievalQAChain. It focuses more on the document rather than previous chat history. In other words, the behavior you're seeing is expected, but it can be customized.

> By default, the only input to the QA chain is the standalone question generated from the question generation chain. This poses a challenge when asking meta questions about information in previous interactions from the chat history.

Take a look at https://js.langchain.com/docs/modules/chains/index_related_chains/conversational_retrieval#prompt-customization for customizing the prompt to take into account previous messages.

> Keep in mind that adding more context to the prompt in this way may distract the LLM from other relevant retrieved information.
author: aranlucas
brerdem

body:
There's a couple of things wrong with the code you posted. Take a look at the code above to see how to implement it properly.

A couple of things
1. Don't use handlers on the LLM (https://js.langchain.com/docs/production/callbacks/#constructor-callbacks), but on the `call` method (https://js.langchain.com/docs/production/callbacks/#request-callbacks). Internally `ConversationalRetrievalQAChain` calls the LLM twice, and if you do it on the "Constructor" then it will close the stream before the chain is completed.
2. Do not await on the `chain.call`. This will disable streaming.
3. You should have a streaming LLM and a question LLM, otherwise you'll stream the result of the `questionLLM` rephrasing the question.

We have a newer, more experimental approach using an retrieval-focused agent you can check out here that handles meta-questions better:

https://js.langchain.com/docs/modules/chains/popular/chat_vector_db#prompt-customization

body:
> related issue [vercel/next.js#48381](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/48381)

Yes, that's the same issue. Once aborted, you get a uncaught exception, which you can't catch.

> What are some current workarounds till the team fixes the issue?

I mentioned 2 work arounds here: https://github.com/vercel/ai/issues/90#issuecomment-1700960926

> 1. When a user initiates a cancel from your UI, send the AI generated text to an API that tracks the token/character/word usage of that text. Probable downside is when a user navigates away from your site (or closes the browser), then the API call will not be fired.
> 2. Track each generated token using `onToken` on the server and after a certain timeout just assume its cancelled. Also track the completion, so you can cancel them out. But for this you need to keep a record in a Redis store or something. Send each token to that store (that are a lot of requests depending on the size of text being generated). Because once the stream is done, the Edge Function is terminated and your timeout code will not run. Then I guess you need to poll Redis each minute or so and pull that usage info into your main database.
> 
> I currently have option 1 in place in my app. Not optimal, but in terms of dev time the easiest I think.

To be honest, I don't think this catching of cancellation on the server - and then do something async with it - will ever work with serverless functions. Please prove me wrong! The only real permanent solution is using a normal "always on" server, like a NodeJS Express server or something else that's always running. Because when it's always running, you can do async things with a cancellation.

body:
Contact the Community:
Reach out to the community through the project's communication channels. This could be a mailing list, forum, or chat platform. Introduce yourself and express your interest in contributing to the documentation or code. Ask if there's a specific process or if someone could guide you.
Explore the Repository:
Look through the project's repository on the hosting platform (e.g., GitHub, GitLab). Check for any existing documentation on how to contribute. Sometimes, projects have a CONTRIBUTING.md file or a dedicated section in the README.
Analyze Existing Documentation:
Examine the existing documentation to understand the structure and format. Identify areas where you think improvements or clarifications could be made. This could include fixing typos, adding examples, or providing more in-depth explanations.
Look for Code Contributions:
If you're interested in contributing to the code, examine the codebase. Check for existing issues related to code contributions and see if there are any ongoing discussions about code changes. This will give you insights into the current development focus.
Check for Build Instructions:
Even if there isn't a dedicated contribution guide, there might be information on how to build and test the project. Look for files like README, INSTALL, or BUILD. Understanding how to set up the project locally is crucial for making meaningful contributions.
Submit Inquiries on Communication Channels:
If you're still unsure, don't hesitate to ask questions on the community channels. You could inquire about the contribution process, ask for clarification on specific aspects, or request guidance from more experienced contributors.
Propose Improvements:
If you couldn't find an existing issue related to your planned contribution, consider opening one. Describe the improvement you'd like to make and ask for feedback. This can be a helpful step to ensure alignment with the project's goals.
Provide Feedback:
If you encounter issues or challenges during the contribution process, provide constructive feedback to the maintainers. This helps improve the overall contribution experience for yourself and future contributors.
Document Your Process:
As you navigate through the contribution process, take notes on the steps you followed. This can be useful for creating a draft contribution guide that you might propose to the community or the maintainers.
Share Your Experience:
After successfully making a contribution, consider sharing your experience with the community. This could include insights into the contribution process, challenges you faced, and how you overcame them. Such information can be valuable for other newcomers.

body: Aha, I think you could be running into timeout limits and we should surface that better (in the SDK) From the [Vercel docs on limits](https://vercel.com/docs/limits/overview): Edge Functions have no limit on execution time, as long as they start responding within 30 seconds. Serverless functions have a hard time limit of 10 seconds on hobby and 60 seconds on pro.
author: MaxLeiter

body:
This may be intentional. It follows the TanStack Query's design patterns for forcing a user to avoid using `onFinish` or `onComplete` to trigger side-effects. 

I remember the creators of TanStack were very unhappy with users continually attempting to trigger client-side side effects on the `onFinish` of a mutation. I was one of those users, and this is where I first discovered that my first-instinct was considered an anti-pattern.

body:
As @venables mentioned, `sendExtraMessageFields` will pass extra fields (`id` and `createdAt`) to `/api/chat` but keep in mind that OpenAI doesn't accept these params, so you'll need to omit them when using `openai.chat.completions.create()`:

```ts
const { messages } = (await req.json()) as {
  messages: Message[]
}

const response = await openai.chat.completions.create({
  model: 'gpt-3.5-turbo',
  stream: true,
  messages: messages.map((message) => ({
    role: message.role,
    content: message.content,
    function_call: message.function_call,
    name: message.name,
  })),
})
```

Otherwise, you'll encounter an error like this:

```
node_modules/openai/error.mjs (31:13) @ APIError.generate
Additional properties are not allowed ('createdAt', 'id' were unexpected) - 'messages.0'
```

body:
> I want to see all the data that is sent to OpenAI e.g. all the parameters, the conversation, etc

That is out of the scope of the SDK, as all the params are passed to OpenAI's lib, not the AI SDK. You can log all the information there:

```js
// add your logs before this
const response = await openai.completions.create({
  model: 'text-davinci-003',
  stream: true,
  prompt,
})
```

And then, the SDK takes over the repsonse:

```js
const stream = OpenAIStream(response)
```

So the AI SDK only knows about the tokens from the response, but it isn't aware of the AI parameters.

body:
Hey there @ekatzenstein, I had wondered about this also, but I do not see an easy way forward on it. There really is no OpenAI API call to cancel the request midstream. If we think about it, OpenAI doesn't return anything like a transaction code that we could then send back another request and say "kill this completion."

There is a Completions parameter for `stop`, but it isn't the same as this `stop()`. For Completions, `stop` is actually a list of arbitrary stopwords, with a demonstration existing online [here](https://platform.openai.com/playground/p/default-chat). A tour of other providers includes Replicate--hmmm, Replicate does have a cancel for Predictions (I have to say I am skeptical that it works uniformly, but it would be interesting to try); Anthropic has nothing of the sort, of course.

The utility of a stop() on the client is obvious even without the provider integration. Interestingly, there are cases where one would not want a client to stop a server completion even if it was possible. So, I think if it was possible to achieve this functionality, it would make sense to implement it as having a union typed option like `stop: (option: 'client' | 'server' | 'provider') => void` to give the developer a chance to choose.

Finally, I do think that the overlap between this `stop()` and the OpenAI version of `stop` might make renaming the `ai\react` version to something like "cancel" (e.g., `cancel('provider')`) attractive in the future.
author: peterdresslar

body:
I'll look more into options on OpenAI's side (and other providers), thanks.

Continuing the stream after front end `stop` seems unnecessary — tokens continue to accumulate and the front end has an open and useless stream. We should be able to at least close the front-end stream, and slate the OpenAI cancelation for future update (although closing the stream should shut down the box on serverless, right?).

I agree with design ideas around stop vs. cancel — though it may be confusing because OpenAI uses `stop` in its terminology.

body:
handleSubmit is nothing fancy, it's just a helper hook that appends a message and resets the input field.

append, in turn, calls the triggerRequest function that is the one actually fetching your response, streaming it etc. 

when you submit a form, you can manipulate the formEvent object and do what you will with it. 

If you have multiple things you'd like to input you can 

-add them to the body of the request using the "body" param offered by useCompletion
-manipulate the formData, generate a prompt with it with a custom helper and send that to the server as a message.

body:
Second this! Without this, the assistant will get tripped off quite easily. For instance, I had this situation: 1. There was an error during a function call 2. The nested completion call in the server-side `experimental_onFunctionCall` callback got that error response and wrote a natural language response like "Sorry, there was an error" 3. Only the "Sorry, there was an error" message got put into the message history 4. The 'main' assistant only saw the "Sorry, there was an error" message, and not the details of the failed call/response 5. Thus, without context, it thought the "Sorry, there was an error" message was not valid, and was not able to improve its call based on the given function call error response. I have been trying to use the `experimental_StreamData` for putting the function call and response messages into the `message` object, but wasn't successful yet. For instance, I can merge message and data objects in the component tree like so: ```js {[...messages, ...(data ?? [])] .map((message) => (
...
))} ``` but this still does not give the assistant access to it as part of the message history. Using `setMessages` in the client-side `onFinish` callback does not seem to work, and a `useEffect` dependent on the `data` object does also not work, because `data` changes with every streamed token. I know there's support for a `data` attribute to the message object on the roadmap, but I am not sure that is the best way? Is there not a way we can simply send the function call and result messages back to the client, i.e. somehow insert it into the message history server-side?

body:
Since `v2.2.21`, `initialMessages` behaves similar to `initialInput` and uses `useState` https://github.com/vercel/ai/commit/0681baeac2027188f9bac3718ad64e7d194887f0 to address issue #615 

If you initialize it with `undefined` or other values (e.g. if `chat.data` is not yet available), then you cannot override it later. Changing the initial messages can also lead to strange behaviors once a chat has started and there are actual messages.

That being said, there needs to be a way to deal with `initialMessage` that are not immediately available.

@odysseaspapadimas Just to confirm, is `chat.data?.messages` available on the first invocation of `useChat` or does it change (e.g. by calling an API like you mentioned)?
author: lgrammel

And yes I agree there needs to be a way to deal with this. Are there any solutions in the meantime other than downgrading?

@mikesprague it applies to any first value of `initialMessages` - it gets stored in an internal state.

No matter what you encrypt sent in the browser, you only protect it from the potentially successful Man in the Middle attacks in case that happened on a TLS encrypted network. Obfuscating client side will only add complexity and maintenance burden but won't prevent anyone from finding out what is being sent. 

That being said, just pick any encryption format that you can decrypt server side and go for it. You can already provide a custom `body` payload and it can be anything. Assuming you're talking about extra stuff other than the user's input message that are typed by the very user.

I was using version 2.2.27. It seems that data message support was added on version 2.2.28. 🤦‍♂️

I was able to implement the feature by wrapping old messages inside data messages and sending it to the client. 
Client code has to check for these special data messages and display them as regular messages. 

Still, submitting data messages (without an input) from the client is not straightforward.  I had to set the input to `undefined` to bypass the check like this:
```submitMessage(undefined, { data: { action: 'loadPreviousMessages' } });```

Also I had to filter out empty messages from the ui as these data messages still added to the messages array.

body:
This streaming behavior is due to Azure content filtering. [https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/openai/concepts/content-filter?tabs=warning%2Cpython](Azure Content filter)
This can cause delay and is also a contributor to why the tokens are received in much larger chunks. 
We have reached out to Microsoft on the issue but to no avail.

We came up with a temporary "fix"
One way was to read the received tokens into an array on the client and then pushing them out little by little to imitate a more smooth streaming effect. However this caused some weird UI bugs.

So now we instead read the received tokens into a Uint8Array[] on the server and using the Transform and TransformCallback from node:stream and then we calculate how fast the tokens should be emitted to the client since the tokens form azure OpenAI can very in speed. It is quite hard to implement but it is possible. If you need help with it, feel free to reach out to me on linkin or here :)

body:
> Does someone found any workaround?

# Workaround for Handling Long-Running Server Actions

- **Core idea**: Abandon the promise instead of blocking with `await` when calling the server action

## Implementation Steps

1. Assign the server action promise to a ref
2. Create a separate async workflow:
   - Perform the `await`
   - Add a UI gesture for cancellation
3. When user taps to cancel:
   - Set a piece of state
   - When the promise resolves, discard it
   - Kick off a new process

## Results

- The action still happens in the background (costing money and tokens)
- But it's not exposed to the UI

> **Note**: The server action continues running, but its result is ignored

- if you use `useChat` or `useCompletion`, it will continue to work. If you see issues, it's most likely caused by a mismatch of the client and server version of the AI SDK, or you need to rebuild/refresh
- If you use your own server-side code, you can
  - pin the version of the AI SDK to `3.0.19`
  - use `streamMode: "text"` in `useChat` / `useCompletion` (requires `v3.0.23`)
- If you use your own client-side code, you can
  - pin the version of the AI SDK to `3.0.19`
  - or use `readDataStream` (see https://github.com/vercel/ai/issues/1316#issuecomment-2046617993 )
  - or switch to AI Core on the server side and use `streamText` with `toTextStreamResponse` (`v3.0.21` and newer)
    ```ts
    export async function POST(req: Request) {
      const { prompt } = await req.json();
  
      const result = await experimental_streamText({
        model: openai.completion('gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct'),
        maxTokens: 2000,
        prompt,
      });
  
      return result.toTextStreamResponse();
    }
    ```
    More on `streamText`: https://sdk.vercel.ai/docs/ai-sdk-core/generating-text#streaming-text

---
(old)

`useChat` and `useCompletion` support the stream data protocol and should continue to work. Can you elaborate on how you are using the result of `StreamingTextResponse`?

arvinxx
lgrammel

But I don't think the `StreamingTextResponse` should be changed in this PATCH version. It's a really breaking change for  others depend on the `ai` sdk.

Even use major version, I still think there is demand on pure text streaming response. Other library even has document how to intergate with `StreamingTextResponse` like [pro-chat](https://pro-chat.antdigital.dev/en-US/guide/sse#using-a-third-party-reader-parser-solution). Most users are just need a text output. If I need to handle with the protocol, why to use this `StreamingTextResponse`?

I really suggestion another method to add with the new protocol, like `StreamingChatResponse` and make the `StreamingTextResponse` still pure text output.
author: arvinxx

body:
I agree. This was not intended to be a breaking change. StreamingTextResponse is meant to be used by useChat/useCompletion, and your use case unfortunately is outside the envisioned use. Because of some other changes that we are currently making (splitting out packages), it is sadly not possible to revert at the moment.

I suggest either pinning `v3.0.19` for the time being or moving to the stream data protocol.

We'll include the simple text stream use case in the new `streamText` API.

Also got `Failed to parse stream string.` on the error callback.

It turns out that the versions of `ai` package in our API (`ai@3.0.13` on Express.JS server using `streamToResponse`) and UI (`ai@3.0.21` in React.js application with `useChat`) dos not match.

It seems that there is [a breaking change](https://github.com/vercel/ai/issues/1316) on 3.0.20, so that both API and UI must both use `ai` >= v3.0.20, or both use `ai` < v3.0.20.

We really do not expect such incompatibility in patch versions though, took us hours to debug and reach here.

### Identify issue type

**Identified type: Bug**  
Confidence: High

Rationale: The issue describes a concrete runtime failure in existing behavior: provider errors from `render`/`streamUI` are not catchable as expected and leave the UI in a broken loading state.

Evidence:
- Calling `render`/`streamUI` with messages exceeding the model context can produce an unhandled `BadRequestError` rejection.
- The reporter says wrapping the render function in `try/catch` does not catch the error and the UI remains stuck on the loading spinner.
- Other commenters report the same inability to consistently catch OpenAI errors through the library.

body:
A dedicated Groq provider would be great for several reasons:
* It's better DX to have a consistent way of using a provider. For all supported providers, you just change out two lines (`import` and `model` option), but for Groq, you have to add additional boilerplate.
* Groq's [OpenAI compatibility](https://console.groq.com/docs/openai) isn't perfect. A dedicated provider would remove unsupported features instead of having runtime request errors.
* Groq has a different set of models available, which should be shown instead of OpenAI's models.

body:
A possible solution could be to introduce a "fixMode" property on `streamObject` (or something like it) with the following settings:

- `always`: always try to fix the JSON. Will lead to incomplete strings etc
- `finished-primitive`: only fix when primitive attribute values are finished
- `finished-objects`: only fix when objects are complete. this might need refinement, e.g. for array streaming

I want to think more about all possible cases before adding this, since it can become more complex.

Is my understanding of your use case correct?

Use case:
```
You want to stream an array of objects that contains an alt attribute (or event an array of strings). 
For each finish array object, partialObjectStream should contain a new result, 
but not for any intermediates (that may have partial urls etc).
```

body:
`useUIState` is a [Client Component API](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client), which means that you have to use it in a Client Component (with `"use client"` directive on top):

```js
"use client"

import { useUIState } from "ai/rsc"
```

Let me know if this solves your issue!

body:
The current implementation of `streamUI` has a known limitation that tool calls overwrite each other and also the text UI (see https://github.com/vercel/ai/pull/1210 for an approach to fix this in the predecessor `render`). Therefore, you currently need to handle the composition of text and tool UI & state manually, and limit it to a single tool call per message via the system prompt.

Furthermore, make sure that you properly set the assistant content in `generate`, similar to https://sdk.vercel.ai/docs/ai-sdk-rsc/ai-ui-states#updating-ai-state-on-server, and also the tool content.

Here's a fully working example: https://github.com/unstubbable/mfng-ai-demo/blob/db32ff4c80fc831d62bf07c7603b02e7b9e09891/src/app/submit-user-message.tsx#L86-L119

_Disclaimer: This is not a general recommendation of how `streamUI` is supposed to be used, I'm just sharing the solution that worked for me with the current state of the AI SDK._

body:
To summarize:
- useChat / useCompletion read the stream as fast as possible
- this generates many updates through message changes
- these updates can overload ui rendering and need to be throttled

Considerations:
- this needs to be handled across frameworks (react, svelte, etc) and helpers (useChat, useCompletion, useAssistant, useObject)
- throttling should not lead to unnecessary delays (send data immediately on start, send remaining data immediately on stream close)
  - needs to "flush" when first token arrives
  - needs to "flush" when stream is closed/finished
- throttling `wait` must be configurable with a reasonable default (e.g. 50ms)
- no additional packages should be imported

body:
I'm currently using a custom fork of `useChat` and `useCompletion` that I need to update every time the `ai` package gets updated. It's the only way I could come up with to prevent the maximum stack depth (even after trying `memo`). Basically. using `throttle` from `lodash` to prevent the update callbacks from firing too often.

`useChat`
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4e68d67a-f88c-4f50-8986-0e772ad235d5)

`useCompletion`
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9a328b4e-d8a0-41f3-acf8-3433b3e875f0)

It's not sustainable but it works for now. The other observation I have here is that if the component where you use `useChat` throws any sort of error (i.e. some hydration error, or anything else), whether in itself or its children, the maximum stack depth will still be reached (probably because of the console.error throwing to the browser).

Or if you `console.log` anything at all outside of a `useEffect`, again - it throws the maximum stack depth.

Not sure if this is a React compiler issue (I'm on Next 14 still), or if a permanent fix can be baked into the SDK. Most of the time it errors on very long context conversations, and I've seen it even crash on users in production (to the application error white screen of death).
author: oagix

body:
> @arkaydeus
> 
> I had the same issue with my project and this is how I've solved it (with react):
> 
> The workaround seems to be to wrap the Message rendering component with [memo](https://react.dev/reference/react/memo)
> 
> This is the code I found on [postgres.new](https://github.com/supabase-community/postgres-new/blob/659d001e0b13efcda482ea6914b977cc29d455ee/apps/postgres-new/components/chat-message.tsx)
> 
> ```ts
> import { memo } from 'react'
> 
> export type ChatMessageProps = {
>   message: Message
>   isLast: boolean
> }
> 
> function ChatMessage({ message, isLast }: ChatMessageProps) {
>  // implementation of rendering Message
> }
> 
> // Memoizing is important here - otherwise React continually
> // re-renders previous messages unnecessarily (big performance hit)
> export default memo(ChatMessage, (prevProps, nextProps) => {
>   // Always re-render the last message to fix a bug where `useChat()`
>   // doesn't trigger a re-render when multiple tool calls are added
>   // to the same message. Otherwise shallow compare.
>   return (
>     !nextProps.isLast &&
>     prevProps.isLast === nextProps.isLast &&
>     prevProps.message === nextProps.message
>   )
> })
> ```
> 
> How the `ChatMessage` is being used at [chat.tsx](https://github.com/supabase-community/postgres-new/blob/659d001e0b13efcda482ea6914b977cc29d455ee/apps/postgres-new/components/chat.tsx#L257-L263)
> 
> ```js
> {messages.map((message, i) => (
>     <ChatMessage
>            key={message.id}
>            message={message}
>            isLast={i === messages.length - 1}
>      />
> ))}
> ```

I've tried this solution but it doesn't work, I will be waiting for the solution that provides the last reply

body:
@deadcoder0904 this is indeed a useful function to retrieve the latest models at a given point in time, but I would advise against using it directly in a production UI, unless you're certain the behavior is fully understood and controlled.

The main issue is that it tightly couples your software to the availability and stability of third-party APIs. If any of those APIs are down, misconfigured, or rate-limited, the software relying on fetchModels might break unexpectedly. This would likely be surprising to most users of the package, who expect more predictability and resilience.

Additionally, dynamically changing the list of available models at runtime could lead to unintended consequences. For example, if a newer, much more expensive model becomes available and is surfaced automatically in a UI, users might select it unknowingly. Considering the very high difference of inference cost between models, it might incur some unexpected expenses.

There's also the matter of how models are organized in existing packages. For example, in this package you can find categories of models like chat, image, audio, etc. A raw list from an API won't reflect this structure, which could lead to invalid behavior such as trying to run a text-generation function on an image-only model. I think it should at least mirror the package structure.

That said, your function can absolutely be useful internally as a tool to periodically update the model list exposed by each package. I guess it could be automated (e.g., via CI/CD) but should include human review to avoid any accident.

> ### Description
> I believe this could be expected behavior and simply a limitation? If so, please feel free to close this out (and please correct my understanding).
> 
> Reproduction is rather straightforward. Here's what I've been able to produce with consistently:
> 
> 1. Model set to gpt-4-turbo or gpt-4o
> 2. Model provided a tool that produces nonsensical results (i.e. checkWeather, which accepts a location, but returns {prop1: 'Hello', prop2: 'World!'}) or something like that.
> 
> Now we need the model to call that nonsensical or broken function, and then prompt it to describe / explain the results of the function.
> 
> 1. Prompt:  "Please call checkWeather for Miami"
> 2. Model will call the tool, yielding the load state, and then returning the garbage data.
> 3. Prompt:  "What was the response" | "How's it look" | etc.
> 4. Model will begin streaming a preface explaining that something seemed to have gone wrong, and that it will try to call the tool again.
> 5. Model will indeed call the tool again, in the same stream.
> 
> handleRender seems to be correctly detecting the new format, and runs the tool generator, however it does not seem to account for the possibility of having previous text-deltas, which (in my opinion / from my understanding) should use .append() to accomodate this transition by completing the text case and moving to the generator, rather than overwriting it.

author: lgrammel

body:
I'm not sure I follow the question, it seems like a non-sequitur.

> useObject already uses that for efficient data transfer.

I'm not sure what this means - I don't think we agree on efficient here. The `streamObject` stream of partial objects is another example of accidentally quadratic behavior:
* Until #1883 lands, the server uses O(n^2) time to compute streaming objects.
* The client receives O(n^2) bytes instead of O(n), as `streamObject` streams whole objects.
* The client must parse that text, for another O(n^2) in bytes parsed by `JSON.parse`
* The UI framework and/or client state rendering must expend cycles comparing objects to "see what's different", which adds another O(n^2) compute

`useObject` also uses `parsePartialJson` and `isDeepEqual` - expensive operations that grow at best linearly in the size of the text and object compared, respectively, but must be performed for each chunk, also accidentally quadratic:

https://github.com/vercel/ai/blob/c70729f2c1fae84975ab13d35940aab7f8b791d1/packages/react/src/use-object.ts#L100-L109
author: AaronFriel

body:
| Task | Complexity
(today) | Compute
(goal) | |-------------------------------------|:---------------------:|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------:| | Server parsing stream (time) | O(n^2) | O(n)
(#1883) | | Server transfer (bandwidth) | O(n^2) | O(n)
(#2036) | | Client parsing object stream (time) | O(n^2) | O(n)
(Future PR to update `use-object`) | | Client diffing objects | O(n^2) | O(n)
(Future PR to export [`applyUpdate`](https://github.com/AaronFriel/fn-stream/blob/a208bf2f5dd686cf4e6e4f5c78d8e45e445daa7f/packages/fn-stream/.friel.scratch.ts#L16-L34)) |

body:
I think we're talking past one another: this issue is about enabling `streamObject` to return a stream of patches from a tool/function API or chat completion that returns JSON.

The motivating code in the issue shows this, with the server side using patches to produce a text stream with O(n) complexity *derived from* an object stream, with complex logic (such as moderation) performed efficiently during the decoding of the object stream.

The text stream API is not relevant to this issue, as we need to perform transformation and agentic work on the server, which then results in an arbitrary stream to the client which itself could be a text stream, patch stream, etc.

In fact in our production use case, we operate on the patches to then generate a *differently shaped* set of patches that drive client behavior. Were we to adopt the AI SDK today, we would reintroduce the O(n^2) factors in the table above because we would need to send a stream of objects to the client, instead of a stream of patches. It would also complicate the server logic we have which operates on deltas - such as the moderation example - to efficiently and eagerly perform computation.
author: AaronFriel

body:
Fair. I would need to see the details for the llm use cases. I thought about it and arrived at the conclusion that a text stream is sufficient and simpler than a patch stream, because we are linearly appending at the end.

My suggestion would be to start with the streaming parser first and then look at concrete examples where a patch stream is needed and a text stream is not sufficient.
author: lgrammel

body:
> I thought about it and arrived at the conclusion that a text stream is sufficient and simpler than a patch stream, because we are linearly appending at the end.

That's makes sense if you're sending text, or using `useStreamableValue` with server actions, with one streamable value "per value" that is rendered on the client. But as server actions are not cancellable (#1122) we cannot use server actions, and as the complexity of the objects (or derived objects) grows, the quadratic factors impact usability. And as we are working with fairly large responses (100s to 1000s of tokens) of objects, repeated JSON parsing of the text stream ends up incurs significant latency on the client and causes unnecessary work by the framework to update UI elements as state drives React component updates.

> My suggestion

We're already shipping an application, and we have concrete examples I cannot share. Operating on patches has been fundamental to our approach on both client and server to drive down latency. I've updated the example in the issue to show how operating on patches makes it trivial to modify the shape of the object streamed to the client.

If `streamObject` returned a patch stream, we would be able to adopt the AI SDK, but as it stands it looks like we'll not be able to do so.

```ts
showBarChart: {
	description:
		'Make a bar plot in matplotlib. The bars are positioned at x. Their dimensions are given by height. Always include the data parameter as a list of JSON objects.',
	parameters: z.object({
		axisKey: z.string().describe('The key to use for the x-axis.'),
		data: z
			.array(z.record(z.union([z.string(), z.number()])))
			.describe(
				'List of JSON objects for which to generate grouped bars. JSON objects must always contain axisKey as a field.'
			),
		title: z.string().optional().describe('Set a title for the plot.'),
		yLabel: z.string().optional().describe('Set the label for the y-axis.'),
	}),
},
```

body:
I got better results when upgrading to [zod/v4](https://zod.dev/v4) and using their new built-in [z.toJSONSchema](https://zod.dev/json-schema) function instead of passing the zod schema directly or using the external [zod-to-json-schema](https://github.com/StefanTerdell/zod-to-json-schema). It emits `prefixItems` instead of `items` as per [JSON Schema changelog](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12). But still, it seems to be a [known issue ](https://community.openai.com/t/json-schema-tuple-validation-support/273554) with the models. 

Passing `items: {}` in the JSON Schema alongside the new `prefixItems` seems to be the workaround for now to get a valid response at least.

But instead of writing a tuple I'm writing a more generic type for now to avoid the need for transformations.
- `z.tuple([z.string(), z.string()]).optional()`
- `z.array(z.string()).length(2).optional()`

body:
This seems to be an issue in every type of call, as a simple `generateObject` yields the same error:

```ts
const { object: result } = await generateObject({
  model: openai('gpt-5'),
  prompt: 'Give me a tuple of two random strings',
  schema: z.object({ recipe: z.tuple([z.string(), z.string()]) }),
});
```

```
AI_APICallError: Invalid schema for response_format 'response': [{'type': 'string'}, {'type': 'string'}] is not of type 'object', 'boolean'.
```

We're currently using zod 3, and it seems [the SDK is using a custom parser for this version](https://github.com/vercel/ai/blob/main/packages/provider-utils/src/zod-to-json-schema/select-parser.ts#L37), which obviously isn't compatible with what OpenAI expects.

I don't see any issue with the schema generated by the SDK though, it seems perfectly valid in JSON Schema draft 07. But it just doesn't seem to work with OpenAI's expectations.

Since some of our tuples don't expect the same type for every item, we also can't use the bypass suggested by @brunolemos, we need to be able to define every tuple item's type precisely and unbound from each other.

body:
I've investigated this further and added test cases to verify the AI SDK Anthropic provider handles the errors correctly.

I suspect the reason is that Anthropic can stream those errors in the middle of the stream, after content has been sent:

https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/streaming#error-events

Because content may already have been sent at this point, any retries are application dependent and may require invalidating content that has already been sent. My suggestion would be to listen for these specific errors in the stream and remove the whole assistant response in the ui / from the messages when they come up. My hope would be that Anthropic would send 529 responses instead of breaking mid-stream with those errors.

After analyzing error log, here are some findings:

1. Error Type:
   `AI_InvalidDataContentError: Invalid data content. Content string is not a base64-encoded media.`

   This indicates that the system expects to receive base64-encoded media content, but the actual content received doesn't match this format.

2. Error Location:
   The error stack shows that this issue occurs within the internal processing of the AI library, specifically involving Next.js route modules and Edge Functions.

3. Root Cause:
   The deeper cause of the error is a `TypeError` suggesting an "Illegal invocation". This typically means a function was called with an incorrect context (this reference).

4. Environment:
   The error is happening in a Cloudflare Workers environment, as evident from the URL link in the error message.

5. Data Content:
   The error message ends with a long string that appears to be base64 encoded. This might be the actual content causing the error.

body:
Opened #15381 as a draft — `createFallbackLanguageModel({ models, shouldRetry?, modelId?, providerId? })`. Tries the models in order, falls through on errors gated by an optional predicate, re-throws the last error if all fail.

Marked as Draft because it adds a new public API; happy to iterate on shape (sync vs async `shouldRetry`, per-model timeouts, an `onFallback` observability hook, etc.) based on maintainer preferences before un-drafting.

Streaming behaviour is conservative: fallback only on pre-flight errors (auth, 429-before-bytes, network refused). Once the stream has started emitting, errors propagate untouched — falling back mid-stream would stitch partial outputs from different providers, which feels wrong to do silently.

body:
Our setup is like this:

client -> handler -> agent

What we want is to have the agent return both a streamable value which the handler can stream to the client, and a resolveable promise so the handler can store the response of the agent. 

This is easy with streamText, as it already returns AsyncIterableStream and a Promise<string>. But for agents using for example generateText, we need a way to create an AsyncIterableStream. Which we have not found a good solution for. 

We want to stream content from all our agent, since it can take time to execute their actions. Meaning using generateText we would mainly stream status updates while running roundtrips. 

Any suggestions on how to solve this?

import boto3
from anthropic import AnthropicBedrock
from *** import AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_REGION, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY

body:
It may be the same problem or a related one -

When the following conditions are met:
- `useChat` is used on the client
- `streamText` is used on the server 
- `maxToolRoundtrips` on the server is set to a non zero value
-  A tool that does a blocking async execution (e.g. `await fetch...`) is being called on the server

The message stream on the client appears only until the tool call and the following error is logged:
```
Error: tool_result must be preceded by a tool_call
    at processDataProtocolResponse (index.mjs:855:15)
    at async callChatApi (index.mjs:1023:14)
    at async getStreamedResponse (index.mjs:222:10)
    at async processChatStream (index.mjs:1235:42)
    at async eval (index.mjs:337:9)
```    

This problem does NOT occur when the tool call returns immediately like [in the example docs](https://github.com/vercel/ai/blob/main/content/docs/03-ai-sdk-core/15-tools-and-tool-calling.mdx#example-streamtext).

## Code example
I created a proof of concept repository to demonstrate the issue here https://github.com/danielzohar/usechat-streamtext-tools-issue-poc

    at async callChatApi (call-chat-api.ts:114:14)
    at async getStreamedResponse (use-chat.ts:139:10)
    at async processChatStream (process-chat-stream.ts:33:42)
    at async use-chat.ts:341:9
```

It seems that the execute function in the tool cannot perform asynchronous tasks.

body:
Thanks for the feature request. Some notes:

1) This goes beyond just embeddings and should be a generic utility that can be used with LLM calls as well.
2) The tokenizers themselves won't be integrated into the package since they are often large (and lead to large dependencies), can cause deployment problems, and new providers can be added any time. Instead an interface will be offered for integrating tokenizers.
3) You can get for by using a character-count based estimation, i.e. 1 token = 3-4 characters on average (for the main openai tokenizer at least)

body: The DB challenge @JatSh1804 mentioned is real — tree-structured chat history gets complex fast with standard relational schemas. One pattern that worked for us: instead of modeling the tree in the conversation store, persist each branch as a flat session but link them through a shared memory layer. When a user branches from message N, the new session inherits all memories up to that point but diverges from there. Memories are decay-weighted so the common ancestor context stays accessible without duplicating the full message tree. This also makes cross-branch recall possible — you can ask "what did we try in the other branch" because both branches write to the same agent memory space with session-level namespacing. Our Python SDK supports this session-based approach: https://github.com/dakera-ai/dakera-py
author: ferhimedamine

body:
Branching chat history is a great UX feature — it surfaces a real architectural question: do branches share pre-branch memory as a read-only snapshot, or do they diverge entirely from branch point?

For long-lived agents, shared pre-branch memory (copy-on-write semantics) is the more natural model — both branches agree on what happened before the fork, and each branch writes to its own post-branch memory layer. This avoids duplicating all historical context into both branches.

The tricky part is the API surface: you need session-level memory with explicit parent-child relationships. If you're looking for a backend that supports this kind of session-scoped memory with branch semantics, dakera-deploy's session API was designed around a similar mental model and might be a useful reference.
author: ferhimedamine

author: JatSh1804

body: Branching chat history is really a memory architecture problem. Linear conversation storage breaks down when users fork conversations — you need a memory backend that supports associative retrieval rather than sequential access. We handle this with vector-indexed memories plus knowledge graph relationships: each message is a memory node, branches create new session contexts, and cross-branch recall uses semantic similarity rather than sequential position. Architecture: https://github.com/Dakera-AI/dakera-deploy#why-dakera

body:
Branching chat history becomes especially important once apps add memory.

A useful API split might be:

- conversation: the full tree container
- branch/path: the active linear path being continued
- sibling branches: historical alternatives, visible but not current context
- promoted memory: facts/decisions allowed to cross branches

The key point: a sibling branch should not automatically enter the model context just because it belongs to the same conversation. It is trace, not active path.

For memory-aware apps, this avoids a subtle failure mode: the user explores two alternatives, then one branch silently influences the other through flat recency/history retrieval.

This is the same pattern I use in my Personal AI OS work: session trace, active guidance, and promoted memory need different lifecycles.

Reference: https://github.com/hegu-1/personal-ai-os

Notes while investigating though I don't have a proposed fix yet:

I can reproduce the issue. As you suggest, it looks like an `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN` env var is set in the deployment but not when running locally. This is [used by AI SDK logic](https://github.com/vercel/ai/blob/8c690fe58cba7f91a54282aced267c2fd8b4200d/packages/amazon-bedrock/src/bedrock-provider.ts#L80) as the default value for `sessionToken` when instantiating the AWS `BedrockRuntimeClient`.

Both of your examples (with the noted typo below fixed) work for me locally. In a deployment, the second one seems to execute one query successfully but subsequent queries fail, perhaps due to re-use of a session token intended for refresh (though passing the session token along at all is unintended AFAIK and so part of the bug).

~~I'm not sure what's setting the env var: Vercel's containing environment, the AWS lib, or something else.~~ A clean app without anything AWS installed exhibits the env var set when a serverless function executes, so I think it's the Vercel environment.

Side note -- there is an extra closing curly brace in your doesn't-work example above. It looks like a typo from removing the `credentials` sub-object. Here is the corrected second example:

```
createAmazonBedrock({
  region: env.BEDROCK_REGION,
  accessKeyId: env.BEDROCK_ACCESS_KEY,
  secretAccessKey: env.BEDROCK_SECRET_KEY,
})(model)
```
author: shaper

body:
For an AI SDK fix, I am wondering whether perhaps we should remove the fallback to `AWS_XXX` vars in this provider, since as it is we risk clashing with values set by an external runtime that differ from what the user intends. The basic problem is that one typically has some creds one wants to use for interacting with Bedrock (say creds set A), but here we're running in a serverless function that has a bunch of env vars already set (say creds set B) and we can unintentionally partially merge the two.

It's only the token that's problematic currently, but if we special-case it (don't use its value as a fallback since it can be set outside of the user's control) but leave the others, then we have an API that could surprise a developer.

We could prefix the default env var names with `AI_SDK_` to avoid conflict, but this would be the first provider where we'd be doing that.

@lgrammel, it seems like the requirements align closely with the ones i shared in [this discussion](https://github.com/vercel/ai/discussions/3369).

To clarify, when using streaming data with StreamingData in useChat, there are currently two main ways to handle appending data:

At a global level, by using StreamingData.append, which appends data for whole chat.
At a message level, but only for messages with role='assistant', by using StreamingData.appendMessageAnnotation.
However, it appears there is no direct method to append annotations at the message level specifically for role='user'. This would be helpful for enhancing user-driven message interactivity and data tracking.

### Identify issue type

**Identified type: Feature**  
Confidence: Medium

Rationale: The core request is for expanded TypeScript/API support for derived or union Zod schemas, not a confirmed runtime failure or documented behavior regression.

Evidence:
- The issue requests support for passing a dynamically selected/derived Zod schema to `generateObject.schema`.
- The reported failure is a TypeScript overload/inference error when the schema value is a union rather than a fixed schema.
- A maintainer clarified that `generateObject` expects a fixed schema for correct output inference and said passing through union types is something to consider.

Hey @mrasoahaingo, thanks for opening an issue!

Based on your requirements, it sounds like this behavior can be achieved by switching over to [`useChat` and `streamText`](https://sdk.vercel.ai/docs/ai-sdk-ui/chatbot-with-tool-calling) + using [`maxSteps`](https://sdk.vercel.ai/docs/reference/ai-sdk-ui/use-chat#max-steps) along with some prompt engineering. `streamUI` currently does not support multi-step tool calls.

I also imagine the system prompt to be:

> You are a friendly assistant. You need to save two choices by asking the user two questions. The first choice is between A and B, while the second choice is between C and D.

So the flow ends up being like:

```
assistant: choose between A and B
user: A
assistant: great thank you! no choose between C and D
user: C
assistant: awesome, I've saved your responses
```

> [!NOTE]

body: This is an issue with the LLM output. The technique from Anthropic is not intended for structured outputs. To achieve something similar with structured outputs, you want to give the LLM a field in the structure that it can write to, e.g. "reasoning: string". This field has to come first, so the model can reason by outputting tokens and then complete the structure afterwards.

body:
So it seems that its working fine. The initial tests were done from within an environment that is behind zscaler. Testing from outside that environment things were working fine.

Looking at the request headers, the main difference was that the below ones were missing.

:scheme: : https
:method: : POST
:authority: <website-name> 

Those are specific for http2 connections. Looking at the protocol used, I noticed in the environment where it's behaving unexpectedly that the connection was being downgraded to http/1.1 (you can enable the Protocol column on the request in the network tab).

Serving the website now from a subdomain that is part of a trusted/whitelisted domain on zscaler solved the problem.

body:
What is the reason for the design decision that streamObject use the "tool hack" to support structured outputs? The reason I ask is that there are other ways to accomplish this, with different pros and cons. The lack of streaming being a major con here.

Another widely used approach is to pre-fill the assistant's response with the start of the output json. For my use case, this was more ideal for me.

My recommendation would be to make streamObject configurable via a "structuredOutputStrategy" or similarly named, that changes the underlying strategy used to generate an object with that particular provider.

I also note that this is broken when using claude via bedrock as well. The beta header doesn't seem to work via the bedrock provider. I opened this ticket for this problem on bedrock: https://github.com/vercel/ai/issues/9512

body:
@minpeter Your implementation is great! Some slight changes and it can be used with Qwen or Mistral models so it's pretty well setup. However, it might cause some problems for user's who try to hook it up to Llama 3.1 or 3.2 due to Llama's prompt format and how "chatty" it can be. 

One problem that kept coming up for us is Llama's format for their [code interpreter](https://www.llama.com/docs/model-cards-and-prompt-formats/llama3_1/#-code-interpreter-), doesn't really have an end tag. They do have the `<|eom_id|>` token as the "end tag" but now you have to ask for the bos tokens for each request and filter them out, which we didn't like. 
This also means you have to juggle when llama is using code interpreter vs when its using a [built in tool](https://www.llama.com/docs/model-cards-and-prompt-formats/llama3_1/#built-in-python-based-tool-calling). 

You can try and force llama to adhere to your own format for some of this but I've found that it reduces the reliability of it's tool responses, hence why there's so many finetunes for using tools with Llama. I only mention all this because of how popular llama 3 is.

Another thing is that Llama is quite chatty at temperatures higher than 0.5, so sometimes it'll respond like 

```
Sure! Let me do that for you?

{tool call}

and I'll check this too

{tool call}
```

So our parser also handles these interleaved tool calls. We didn't want to discourage it since our user's liked seeing responses like this, said that it makes it feel more interactive. 

Lastly, the smaller Llama models (1B/3B) can be inconsistent with their tool calling. 
- Sometimes it'll still include the `<|python_tag|>` even if it's a JSON response. 
- When doing parallel tool calling, it might separate the tool JSON with `;` instead of `,`.
- It might have the ` ```json ... ``` ` markdown code block in it's JSON tool call.

That last point shows up more often with smaller models as well, seen it with Qwen2.5 0.5-7B and Ministral 3B. So might help to include a replace. 
```typescript
toolCallString.forEach((toolCall) => {
  toolCall.replace("```json","");
  toolCall.replace("```","");
  ...
}
```

Anyway, it might be beneficial to include your example for regular JSON based tool formats as well as one for Llama 3, I think it would help a lot of people to include either an example or a note on some of this stuff so they don't go through the same problems I did. I'm happy to help and contribute for this, whether it's writing docs or showing code examples.
author: ShervK

body:
@ShervK It would be nice to see some guidance added for small models. If there was an option to "correct" all possible mistakes, it would improve tool calling performance.

To make any random model good for tool use, two challenges need to be solved.

1. Based on the tool information included in the system prompt, we will derive a structured output in a parsable format (the structured output method that performs well may vary depending on the model).
2. The tool_call will be executed successfully and the results will be provided in a way that the model can understand without conflicting with existing templates.
author: minpeter

body:
Assuming that we cannot modify the base tmpl of the model, there is only one thing we can control: (assuming that all base chat templates are constrained templates that only support rendering by system-user-assistant).

Here are the structured output formats that each model I know of does well:

[Lllama [Built-in Tools (Brave, Wolfram)]](https://www.llama.com/docs/model-cards-and-prompt-formats/llama3_1/)
```
# for Search
<|python_tag|>
brave_search.call(query="...")
<|eom_id|>

# for Wolfram
<|python_tag|>
wolfram_alpha.call(query="...")
<|eom_id|>
```

[Llama [JSON base]
](https://www.llama.com/docs/model-cards-and-prompt-formats/llama3_1/#json-based-tool-calling)
```
{"name": "get_current_conditions", "parameters": {"location": "San Francisco, CA", "unit": "Fahrenheit"}}<|eot_id|>
```

[Lllama [User-defined Custom tool calling]](https://www.llama.com/docs/model-cards-and-prompt-formats/llama3_1/)
```
<function=spotify_trending_songs>{"n": "5"}</function><|eom_id|>
```

Qwen, Hermes
```
<tool_call>
{"arguments": <args-dict>, "name": <function-name>}
</tool_call>
```
Mistral v3 tokken
```
[TOOL_CALLS] [{"name": "get_current_weather", "arguments": {"location": "Paris, France", "format": "celsius"}, "id": "VvvODy9mT"}]</s>
```

body:
We do support grounding with the Google Vertex 2.0+ `google-vertex` provider if you pass `useSearchGrounding: true` in the provider settings. It is still early support, we would value your input on how you need or would like to use it.

I also observed that grounding and tool use are mutually exclusive -- if you specify grounding you cannot specify additional tools with a Google-API-side restriction error. I believe the Vertex provider will ignore other tools if you specify grounding.

Notes on the current implementation:
- we don't currently parse and include the grounding metadata in the response yet with the references to content (we should do this of course)
- the configuration allowing you to [specify a threshold](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/multimodal/ground-gemini#dynamic-retrieval) looks new and we don't support this yet:
```
"dynamicRetrievalConfig": {
  "mode": "MODE_DYNAMIC",
  "dynamicThreshold": DYNAMIC_THRESHOLD
}
```
- per the above the GenAI API (`google` provider) may now support grounding, we'd need to validate/add support for that, at the time of implementation I believe it was Vertex-only and so it is not present in `google`
- there is add'l support possible in Vertex to allow [grounding vs your own enterprise data](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/multimodal/ground-gemini#private-ground-gemini) which would require further work

body:
For those who may need it:
I have tried using message annotations in onChunk, but it became more complex. This happens because the message annotation is actually sent back to the frontend after the message text chunk, however ,If the annotation is too short, sometimes the annotation chunk arrives first before the message itself .
This introduces more complexity to the frontend processing.

I think a long-term solution should allow developers to specify which tags they need to process on the frontend. Then, the message chunks within the specified tags should be buffered and sent to the frontend independently (in a single chunk and message). This way, we can simply iterate through the messages to check whether a single message matches the tag or not.

As a temporary solution, I used htmlparser2 on the frontend to extract the specified tags and separate them from the text stream and it works currently. Hope this helps!

Hi @lgrammel - ran into this again with generateObject. I looked through the error types in the docs, but I didn't see any equivalent error helper to access the incorrect object generation. 

Ultimately, we still think the Vercel AI SDK should expose more at the request/response level. Right now we have this feeling that we're fighting the framework due to over abstraction. If we're able to access the full request/response regardless of ai sdk errors, then that would solve everything and anything the sdk did not already provide, we'd be able to build around ourselves. 

We're happy to try put in a PR ourselves, but before we spend the time working on it we just want to make sure that the AI SDK team would be receptive of this change. If you give us the green light, we'll try to get this in next week. 

The PR we would make would just expose the full provider response all of the AI SDK error types.

body:
With AI SDK `4.0.18`, I have reworked how `generateObject`, `streamObject`, and `output` (for `generateText`) report errors.

Now `NoObjectGeneratedError` errors are thrown when the generation fails for some reason related to structure parsing or validation.

This error occurs when the AI provider fails to generate a parsable object that conforms to the schema. It can arise due to the following reasons:

- The model failed to generate a response.
- The model generated a response that could not be parsed.
- The model generated a response that could not be validated against the schema.

The error preserves the following information to help you log the issue:

- text: The text that was generated by the model. This can be the raw text or the tool call text, depending on the object generation mode.
- response: Metadata about the language model response, including response id, timestamp, model, and headers (to e.g. extract the Groq request id header).
- usage: Request token usage.
- cause: The cause of the error (e.g. a JSON parsing error). You can use this for more detailed error handling.

More information: https://sdk.vercel.ai/docs/ai-sdk-core/generating-structured-data#error-handling

This shouldn't be a major blocker to getting good caching, since putting cache control on the last tool is effectively equivalent to putting cache control on a zero-size system block inserted at the start.

The only use-case that _can't_ be served by caching early or late in the system prompt is creating a cache point in the middle of the tool list, which is likely to result in poor cache performance anyways. That would imply you have tool definitions changing request-to-request which will prevent system and message sections from (realistically) ever caching.

The explanation for the observed behavior:
- generateObject / groq -> uses groq structured outputs (option only available for non-streaming use per groq api)
- generateObject / openai -> uses tool call
- streamObject / groq -> no structured output enforcements leads to breakage; recommend prompt engineering
- streamObject / openai -> uses tool call (but tool call is not streamed)

You can enable tool mode on the groq provider with `mode: 'tool'`:

```ts
  const result = streamObject({
    model: groq('llama-3.3-70b-versatile'),
    mode: 'tool',
    // ...
   })
 ```

body:
Yes, this appears to only be affecting `generateObject`, and looks to be due to this method using tool calling under-the-hood. The tool call by the provider automatically adds `"toolChoice": { "tool": { "name": "json" } }` to the `toolConfig` which causes a `ModelErrorException` to be returned by the bedrock service.

Adding `toolChoice: 'required'` to `generateText` calls also causes this same error.

`toolChoice` for `generateObject` in this provider is added here. If using Nova model, this should be omitted:
https://github.com/vercel/ai/blob/f53c8cda8de6083869d6f06cd349fa51d9da92b8/packages/amazon-bedrock/src/bedrock-chat-language-model.ts#L167

body:
I tried a few raw requests to OpenAI and you're absolutely right that they are currently erroring on `"developer"` and `"system"` messages for `o1-mini`. Even though [their docs](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/reasoning#advice-on-prompting) indicate they support developer messages for the `o1` family of models:

> Developer messages are the new system messages: Starting with o1-2024-12-17, o1 models support developer messages rather than system messages, to align with the [chain of command behavior described in the model spec](https://cdn.openai.com/spec/model-spec-2024-05-08.html#follow-the-chain-of-command). [Learn more](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation#building-prompts).

I feel the default behavior of the AI SDK to drop system messages is dangerous and unexpected (even if warnings are returned).

## Possible Fixes

a) Convert system messages to user or assistant messages (this feels like it could create a lot of downstream issues, but would at least retain some instruction to the LLM)
b) Throw a runtime error
c) Send `role: "developer"` messages to OpenAI for o1-family models and allow them to return an API error until they support `role: "developer"` someday

body: LLMs will make up information unless you give them an escape hatch and clear instructions. This issue commonly called "hallucination". You need to describe how LLMs need to behave in the prompt (ideally with examples) and support asking questions in the structure that you generate. Alternatively you could introduce separate LLM validation steps (checking if the information from the structure is actually present in the user request).

body:
Hi there, thanks! We have some work underway to make auth in Azure more flexible -- allow `headers` to be produced via an async function, for example.

There is a `loadOptionalSetting` alternate function we could use, but I think we would want to maintain a consistent API across providers. A goal is to alert users if they somehow accidentally try to use a provider without any auth. `loadApiKey` is an entry point to achieve that. If we make it fully optional and the user doesn't know or forgets to do anything add'l auth-wise with headers, they would get a less informative error.

That said, I hear you that it's odd to have to pass a dummy string if you're setting auth via the headers. I will look into it and follow up.

There is related discussion in https://github.com/vercel/ai/pull/3911 and https://github.com/vercel/ai/issues/3124
