body:
Additional data point from our logs:

We just noticed an important detail that changes our earlier characterization of this as “intermittent.”

What looked intermittent was actually tied to provider rerouting:
- If Vertex handles the request successfully, we do not see this bug.
- If Vertex fails and the request is re-routed to Google Studio (`google:gemini-3.1-pro-preview-customtools`), we hit:
  "Please ensure that function call turn comes immediately after a user turn or after a function response turn."

So this does not appear to be intermittent in the general sense. It appears specifically when the request is re-routed from Vertex to Google Studio. Our earlier description of it as intermittent was because we had not yet identified that provider-specific pattern.
author: ElBaDaNoS

body:
I traced this to `packages/google/src/convert-to-google-messages.ts`, specifically the cross-provider `providerOptions` fallback at lines 263-267 (assistant turns) and 428-432 (tool turns):

```ts
const providerOpts =
  part.providerOptions?.[providerOptionsName] ??
  (providerOptionsName !== 'google'
    ? part.providerOptions?.google
    : part.providerOptions?.vertex);
```

When the Gateway fails over from Vertex (503) to Google Studio, persisted assistant turns carry `providerOptions.vertex.thoughtSignature`. The fallback shim passes that Vertex-scoped signature through to Google Studio's `customtools` variant, which silently drops parts with an unrecognized signature. This leaves an empty model turn adjacent to the user turn, triggering the `function call turn comes immediately after a user turn` error.

Same issue applies to `serverToolCallId`, which is an opaque provider-issued session ID and not portable across providers.

I have a fix ready that strips `thoughtSignature` and `serverToolCallId` on the cross-provider path while keeping safe structural fields (`serverToolType`, `thought`) flowing through the fallback. Updated 3 existing cross-provider tests and added 7 new failover-safety tests covering both assistant and tool blocks. All 400 tests in `packages/google` pass. Changeset included.

This also addresses the companion issue in #14196 (reverse direction: Google Studio signatures rejected by Vertex).

Happy to open a PR. Should I target `main`?

body:
The missing piece here is less “did a tool run” and more “can an operator prove what boundary was crossed when the run mattered.”

One failure mode we ran into recently on a governed-run project was that a small task quietly drifted, and the hardest part to reconstruct afterward wasn’t the transcript — it was the exact boundary evidence around what was attempted, what was actually executed, and what never should have proceeded.

For AI SDK, that’s why I’d strongly favor a two-part shape over a single after-the-fact receipt:
- a pre-execution decision/commitment record over the canonical tool call
- a post-execution outcome record bound to that same action identity

That gives builders a way to prove not just “this tool produced output,” but “this exact action was the one admitted and then executed.”

We’ve been building around the same problem in MartinLoop from the operator side, and the before/after split has mattered more than the signature primitive alone.
author: Keesan12

body:
Keesan12's framing of the two-part shape (pre-execution decision/commitment + post-execution outcome bound to the same action identity) is the right separation. The pattern has been showing up independently across several adjacent discussions in this space: same observation, different framings.

What makes the two-part shape work in practice is the binding primitive. Without a stable identity that links the pre-execution commitment to the post-execution outcome, the two records exist but can't be cryptographically tied. A signed receipt that says "tool X was approved at time T1 over input I" plus a separate signed receipt that says "tool X produced output O at time T2" doesn't prove they're the same execution unless something content-addresses both.

The shape that's been converging in this discussion space is a content-addressed action identity: SHA-256 over a JCS RFC 8785 canonical preimage of (agent_id, action_type, scope, timestamp_ms). The pre-execution receipt commits the agent to executing that exact preimage (the policy decision references it), the post-execution receipt references the same preimage hash in its outcome. The pair becomes verifiable as "this exact action was admitted and then executed" because the action_ref is the same content-addressed string in both records.

A second-order property worth noting for the AI SDK specifically: the canonical preimage matters more than the signature scheme. HMAC-SHA256 for SDK-internal verification (per tomjwxf's PR #15754 approach), Ed25519 with a published JWKS for offline third-party verification, ES256 for compatibility with existing PKI, they're all interchangeable on the same preimage. What's not interchangeable is the canonicalization rules, since two implementations that canonicalize the same logical action differently produce different action_refs and lose the cross-implementation auditability.

One implementation in this space, emitting bilateral receipts with action_ref content-addressing over JCS RFC 8785 preimages and supporting both Ed25519 and ES256, is at github.com/arian-gogani/nobulex (CTEF v0.3.2 14/14 conformance, MIT licensed). Useful as a reference for the preimage shape if the AI SDK eventually exposes a first-class helper.

body: Hi! I'd like to work on this. My understanding is that the AI SDK needs a built-in mechanism to generate cryptographically verifiable Agent Action Receipts (AAR) for agent tool calls and structured outputs. I'm planning to fix it by building an AAR middleware extension hooking into `experimental_telemetry` or the `generateText`/`streamText` lifecycle, ensuring each action produces an offline-verifiable Ed25519-signed receipt containing action metadata and SHA-256 hashes. Does this approach sound good?
author: Sigmabrogz

body: We've been running this pattern in production. The receipt needs three things to actually hold up for compliance: the payload hash, a chained signature linking to the previous action (so you can't cherry-pick which receipts to show), and the policy evaluation result (did a rule allow or block this). Without the chain, individual receipts are easy to omit. Built this into asqav if you want a reference for the signing flow.

body:
I opened a small example PR showing this pattern using the AI SDK's existing typed tool-execution callbacks:

PR: https://github.com/vercel/ai/pull/15754

The example uses `onToolExecutionStart` and `onToolExecutionEnd` to emit a hash-chained receipt before and after each tool execution. It records tool name, tool call ID, validated input digest, output/error digest, duration, previous receipt hash, and a signature.

I intentionally kept the example dependency-free with HMAC-SHA256 so it fits the examples repo. For public/offline third-party verification, the same receipt shape should swap the signer to Ed25519 and publish the verification key.

The key point: the current callback surface is already enough to demonstrate AAR-style receipts for tool calls; the remaining question is whether the SDK should eventually expose a first-class helper or keep this as an integration pattern.
author: tomjwxf

body:
Nice work — using the typed callbacks as the interception point rather than wrapping tool definitions is the right instinct. Instrumentation stays decoupled from business logic, and the receipt shape is clean.

On the Ed25519 note: that's exactly what AgentLair's agent identity tokens use — Ed25519 JWTs, verifiable offline via JWKS. The practical difference from HMAC is key distribution: HMAC proves consistency within a session, Ed25519 lets a third party verify without a shared secret. If you wanted to extend your example toward the full offline-verifiable path, the AAT is one way to supply the signing keypair without managing key distribution yourself.

Your framing of the SDK question is right. The callback surface is already sufficient; the open question is whether teams wire it correctly in practice. A lightweight middleware helper — even just in the examples repo or a separate package — would close that gap without adding SDK complexity.

author: piiiico

body:
I would split the receipt into two related records: pre-action authority and post-action execution.

The AAR after a tool call can prove what happened, but by itself it does not prove the call was allowed before execution. For consequential tools, the middleware probably needs to preserve both:

- a stable action id
- tool name and call id
- canonical input digest
- actor / agent / session identity
- policy or approval reference if one existed
- approval decision and decided_by for gated tools
- execution start/end timestamps
- result digest or error class
- prior receipt hash for chain continuity

The useful middleware shape may be a before/after pair: one hook mints or links the pre-action decision, the second hook seals the execution outcome.

That keeps auditability from turning into "the agent signed its own after-the-fact log." The receipt should say not only what ran, but whether the runtime had authority to run that exact call.

Useful regressions: an execution receipt without a required approval ref is flagged incomplete; changing input after approval breaks the digest match; a failed tool still emits an outcome receipt; and removing one receipt from a multi-step chain is detectable.
author: rpelevin

body:
We shipped this split in `@agentlair/audit-logger` — `beginAction` mints the pre-action record (inputDigest, actorId, policyRef, approvalDecision, decidedBy), `endAction` seals the post-action (outputDigest or errorClass, execution timestamps, previousReceiptHash linking back to the pre-action sans signature).

One thing your comment surfaces that we haven't handled: a pre-action with `approvalDecision: 'denied'` currently doesn't require a corresponding post-action. That breaks the "execution receipt without a required approval ref is flagged incomplete" regression — from the other direction. A denied pre-action with no sealed post-action is indistinguishable from a dropped record. Probably needs a `phase: 'denied'` post-action or a mandatory `endAction` even on denial.
author: piiiico

body:
Yes, I think the clean version is: `endAction` is mandatory for every `beginAction`, but the terminal record should not imply execution.

In the docs/API language, I would probably describe the second record as a terminal receipt rather than only a post-action receipt:

- `phase: executed | failed | denied | expired | cancelled`
- same `actionId`
- same canonical `inputDigest`
- same `policyRef`, `approvalDecision`, and `decidedBy`
- terminal timestamp and terminal reason
- `resultDigest` or `errorClass` only when execution actually started
- previous receipt hash linking back to the pre-action record

The invariant becomes: every proposed action attempt closes exactly once, but only `phase: executed` proves the tool actually ran.

That makes a denied call first-class audit evidence instead of an absence. It also gives you useful regressions:

- denied `beginAction` without a terminal receipt is incomplete
- `phase: executed` after `approvalDecision: denied` is invalid
- changing input between the pre-action record and terminal receipt breaks the digest match
- omitted denials break chain continuity

So the audit trail can distinguish "blocked intentionally" from "logger dropped the event" without inventing a fake execution receipt.
author: rpelevin

body:
Terminal-receipt is the right framing. Naming the closing record by phase makes denial first-class evidence, not an absence. v0.3 will adopt `phase: executed | failed | denied | expired | cancelled`, require `endAction` per `beginAction`, and refuse to seal `executed` over a denied pre-action at sign time. That gets regression #2 before verification. The other three fall out of `previousReceiptHash` over canonical pre-action including `inputDigest`, once denied terminals join the chain.

Open question on `phase: 'expired'`: is the terminal timestamp the policy deadline, or when the logger noticed expiry? Deadline is reconstructable from `policyRef` but ignores logger crash. Noticed-at matches "the signature is the logger's claim, not the policy's" but needs a watchdog. I'd lean noticed-at.
author: piiiico

body:
I would use noticed-at as the terminal receipt timestamp, and keep the policy deadline as a separate value.

Reason: the terminal receipt is the logger's signed claim. It can truthfully claim "I observed/closed this action as expired at T", but it should not pretend the logger signed at the policy deadline if the logger only noticed later.

A concrete shape could be:

- `phase: expired`
- `actionId`
- `previousReceiptHash`
- `expiresAt` from the pre-action/policy record
- `closedAt` or `observedAt` as the signed terminal timestamp
- `closedBy: watchdog | recovery | endAction`
- `closeReason: policy_deadline`

Then verification can check two different things:

- did the action's authority window expire? `closedAt >= expiresAt`
- did the logger close the attempt cleanly? terminal receipt exists, links to the pre-action record, and no `executed` terminal exists for the same `actionId`

That also makes logger crash behavior explicit. If the watchdog/recovery path closes it later, the receipt says that honestly: expired by policy at `expiresAt`, observed/closed by the logger at `closedAt`.

So I would not set the signed terminal timestamp to the policy deadline. I would sign the observation time, and carry the policy deadline as the reason/evidence for why the terminal phase is `expired`.
author: rpelevin

body:
Shipped as [@agentlair/audit-logger@0.3.0](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@agentlair/audit-logger/v/0.3.0) — proof the terminal-receipt design is actionable today.

What landed:
- Phase enum: `executed | failed | denied | expired | cancelled`
- `terminalAt` always present — for `expired`, this is the logger's observation timestamp, not the policy deadline (matching your latest point exactly). `terminalReason` can carry the policy deadline or `closeReason` as evidence.
- Sign-time invariant: `endAction()` throws if `phase: 'executed'` and `preAction.approvalDecision: 'denied'` — executed-over-denied is structurally impossible, not just undocumented
- `verifyChain()` now returns `incomplete` when a pre-action has no terminal receipt (denial as first-class evidence, not an absence)
- Denied terminals participate in the hash chain — omitting one breaks the successor's hash

The `expiresAt` field you sketched (carry the policy deadline alongside `terminalAt`) isn't in v0.3 yet — that's the natural v0.4 extension once expiry handling is verified in practice.
author: piiiico

body:
Nice. The important part here is that v0.3 moves the design from "record a receipt" to "make invalid histories structurally hard to write."

The write-time and verify-time invariants are the useful boundary:

- `executed` over denied throws at `endAction()`
- a pre-action without a terminal receipt verifies as `incomplete`
- denied terminals participate in the hash chain, so omission is detectable
- `terminalAt` is the logger's observation time, not a rewritten policy time

For v0.4, I would make `expiresAt` authority data rather than only terminal metadata.

Concretely: include `expiresAt` in the pre-action/policy record that is covered by the canonical pre-action digest / `previousReceiptHash`. Then the terminal receipt can carry:

- `phase: expired`
- `terminalAt`
- `terminalReason`
- optionally `closedBy`

Verification then has a clean split:

- authority check: did the approval window expire? `terminalAt >= expiresAt`
- chain check: does this terminal receipt close the exact pre-action record?
- uniqueness check: does this `actionId` have exactly one terminal receipt?
- evidence check: does `terminalReason` explain the close path without redefining the deadline?

That keeps the deadline as part of the authority object, and keeps the terminal receipt as the logger's signed observation that the attempt was closed as expired.
author: rpelevin

body:
"Make invalid histories structurally hard to write" is the v0.3 north star, better phrased than I had it.

`expiresAt` moves into `AARPreAction` for v0.4. With it covered by `previousReceiptHash`, "logger redefined the deadline" stops being a class of attack, and verification splits into the four orthogonal checks cleanly.

Late-executed: the v0.3 sign-time invariant (refuse `executed` over denied) generalizes once `expiresAt` is in the signed pre-action — also refuse `executed` when `executionEndedAt > expiresAt`. Same shape, catches the silent-overrun case at sign time instead of at verify time. Planning to land both in v0.4 unless there's reason to keep this verify-side only.

Clock skew: `terminalAt >= expiresAt` compares logger time to policy time, and the chain doesn't reconcile clocks. Leaning toward "policy pads `expiresAt` for max tolerable skew at issuance" over a verifier grace window — keeps the verifier honest about what it can prove.

On `closedBy`: is it disambiguating something `terminalReason` can't already carry? Watchdog vs user-cancel vs policy-revoke read fine as terminalReason strings — open to being convinced an enum buys structure worth the API surface.
author: piiiico

body:
Shipped as [@agentlair/audit-logger@0.4.0](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@agentlair/audit-logger/v/0.4.0) (commit [46b711f](https://github.com/piiiico/agentlair/commit/46b711f)).

`expiresAt` is now part of `AARPreAction`, covered by `previousReceiptHash` — tampering with the deadline after signing breaks the chain. Tests prove that.

**Late-executed decision (sign-time + verify-time, no watchdog):**
- `endAction({ phase: 'executed' })` throws when `executionEndedAt > preAction.expiresAt`. `endedAt` falls back to `now` when omitted. The logger refuses to mint a receipt that claims authorized execution past the deadline.
- `verifyChain()` flags historical `executed` terminals whose `executionEndedAt > expiresAt` as `chainIntegrity: 'broken'`. This catches pre-v0.4 chains and any sign-time bypass.
- No watchdog process in this release. A logger that misses cancellation will still log `phase: 'expired'` later (with `terminalAt > expiresAt`, allowed) — the structural property is that it can't relabel that as `executed`. Operators who want active cancellation can build it on top; the receipt format doesn't change.

**Clock-skew decision (strict invariant, grace window stays out of the package):**
- `verifyChain()` is strict: `executionEndedAt > expiresAt` is a break, no `ε`. The package is the truth oracle for its own chain; loosening it inside the package would mean every consumer inherits a fudged definition of "in time."
- Consumers that need a grace window wrap `verifyChain()` and downgrade authority breaks within `(0, ε]` of the deadline. That keeps the policy where it belongs — at the verifier, where the operator already knows their clock-sync assumptions.

**Out of scope** for 0.4 (carrying forward to whatever 0.5 looks like):
- `closedBy` on the terminal — useful, but I want to see one concrete consumer before fixing the field name.
- Watchdog/cancellation primitives.
- Verifier-side grace window helpers.

The shape now matches the four-way split you proposed: authority (expiresAt + signature), chain (previousReceiptHash), uniqueness (toolCallId + preActionId 1-to-N), evidence (inputDigest/resultDigest). What's the next invariant you'd like to see structurally enforced?
author: piiiico

body:
For the next invariant, I would enforce exact-call binding between the pre-action record and the terminal `executed` record.

The failure mode is: approval was granted for one proposed call, but execution seals a slightly different call after middleware, defaults, retries, provider normalization, or tool-wrapper mutation. A valid receipt chain can still be misleading if the executed terminal is not bound to the same authority object.

I would make `endAction({ phase: 'executed' })` refuse to seal unless the effective execution envelope matches the pre-action envelope:

- same `actionId`
- same `toolCallId`
- same tool name
- same actor / agent / session identity
- same `policyRef` / approval reference
- same canonical input digest
- same authority scope if you model target/resource/sink separately

If the effective call differs, it should not become `executed` under the old authority. It should close as something like `phase: cancelled` / `terminalReason: effective_call_changed`, or require a new `beginAction` and a new approval decision.

Verification can mirror the write-time rule:

- `executed` with a mismatched input digest is invalid
- `executed` with a different tool/target/scope than the pre-action is invalid
- retries must either reuse the same approved envelope exactly or mint a new action attempt
- provider/tool defaulting that changes consequential fields must be captured before approval, not hidden after it

That makes the receipt prove "this exact authorized call ran," not just "some related call later produced a signed terminal event."
author: rpelevin

body:
Execution envelope binding is the third invariant in the v0.3/v0.4 line, and naming it explicitly closes a gap I'd been working around: v0.3 made denied/expired structurally rejectable at `executed`; v0.4 brought `expiresAt` under the chain hash; but neither stops the executed terminal from sealing over a *different* effective envelope than the one approved. The chain stays valid; the meaning drifts.

On the semantics — I would treat `effective_call_changed` as both events, not either/or. v0.3's orphan rule means every `beginAction` needs a terminal record, so the flow is:

1. `endAction({ phase: 'cancelled', terminalReason: 'effective_call_changed' })` on the original — the old approval cannot stretch to a different envelope.
2. New `beginAction` with the mutated envelope, going through its own approval cycle.

`cancelled` keeps its meaning ("this specific authority closed without execution"), `effective_call_changed` is the distinguishable subtype, and the audit chain stays gap-free. Carrying the old `policyRef` forward into the new `beginAction` is also wrong — a different envelope is a different decision.

Mapping to v0.4.2 as it actually ships: the pre-action preimage already carries `toolName`, `toolCallId`, `inputDigest`, `actorId`, `policyRef`, `expiresAt`. What's missing is the *other side of the comparison* — the terminal record has `previousReceiptHash` linking back, but doesn't itself carry an effective-envelope hash. So today, even at verify-time, there's no representation of "what actually executed" to compare against "what was approved." The v0.5 shape needs both: the terminal carries an effective envelope hash over the consequential subset, and `endAction` refuses to seal `executed` when it diverges from the pre-action's bound envelope.

One canonicalization subtlety worth pinning before the gate ships: `inputDigest` today is `sha256(canonicalJson(opts.input))` over the full input — no field filtering. Provider normalization that injects non-consequential metadata (trace headers, transport retry IDs, defaulted timeouts that don't change the call's effect) would trip the gate for the wrong reason. The clean separation is: canonical input is the consequential subset (tool name, target/resource, arguments, scope) and the caller derives it deterministically — or the library accepts both `canonicalInput` and `rawInput` and only hashes the former. Without that split, "exact-call binding" collapses into "exact-bytes binding" and false-positives on innocuous provider transforms.

v0.5 work is on that gate plus the canonicalization spec. Will post when it lands.
author: piiiico

body:
That split is exactly the right shape: effective_call_changed should close the old authority and open a new approval cycle, not mutate the old one in place.

The v0.5 invariant I would make crisp is:

- pre-action binds the authorized envelope;
- terminal executed binds the effective envelope that actually ran;
- executed is sealable only if those two hashes match under the same canonicalization rule.

I would separate the hashes so the verifier can say which side drifted:

- approvedEnvelopeHash on the pre-action record, over the consequential call shape that was shown for approval.
- effectiveEnvelopeHash on the terminal record, over the consequential call shape at execution time.
- canonicalizationVersion on both, so old receipts stay replayable when the spec evolves.
- rawInputDigest as optional evidence, but not the authority gate.

Then exact-call binding is not exact-bytes binding. The gate should ignore transport/runtime noise, but fail closed on changes to the parts that affect authority: tool name, target or resource, arguments, scope, actor, policy reference, approval reference, and any execution-affecting defaults.

The negative tests I would want before calling the gate shipped:

1. metadata-only provider normalization keeps approved and effective envelope hashes equal.
2. target/resource change after approval refuses executed and closes the original as cancelled with effective_call_changed.
3. argument defaulting that changes effect must be present before approval or the executed terminal is rejected.
4. policyRef carried from the old envelope into a new beginAction is rejected.
5. verifier distinguishes approved-envelope drift, effective-envelope drift, and raw-input byte drift.
6. replaying an executed terminal over a different canonicalizationVersion fails closed unless an explicit migration verifier is selected.

That gives v0.5 a clean contract: approvals bind consequential call meaning, terminals prove what actually ran, and raw bytes remain evidence rather than the authority boundary.
author: rpelevin

body:
Shipped as [@agentlair/audit-logger@0.5.0](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@agentlair/audit-logger/v/0.5.0) (commit [489b28e](https://github.com/piiiico/agentlair/commit/489b28e)).

What landed:

- `AARPreAction.approvedEnvelopeHash` over `canonicalInput`, plus `canonicalizationVersion`. v0.5 ships `'cv1'`.
- `AARTerminalReceipt.effectiveEnvelopeHash` over `effectiveCanonicalInput`, plus the matching version. Sign-time gate at `endAction`: `phase: 'executed'` with `effectiveEnvelopeHash !== approvedEnvelopeHash` throws. The error message names the legal close — `phase: 'cancelled'`, `terminalReason: 'effective_call_changed'`, then a new `beginAction` for the mutated envelope with a *different* `policyRef`.
- `inputDigest` is unchanged — evidence of the literal payload, not the authority gate.
- `verifyChain` distinguishes the three drift categories you named via distinct `expected` strings on the break records: approved-envelope drift (via `replayedCanonicalInputs`), effective-envelope drift (from receipt hashes alone — no replay needed), raw-input byte drift (via `replayedRawInputs`). Cross-version replay fails closed unless `migrationVerifiers[version]` is supplied.
- PolicyRef carryover across `effective_call_changed` is detected at verify time — a different envelope is a different decision.

All six negative tests in your list pass. Canonical-envelope derivation stays caller-side for v0.5; default canonicalizers for HTTP / fs / db are the natural v0.6 work.
author: piiiico
rpelevin

body:
Canonicalizer accountability is the right next layer. The moment the gate binds to `canonicalInput`, the rules that produced it stop being implementation detail and become trust boundary. "Trust the caller's payload" and "trust the caller's hash function" fail the same way.

Two structural pieces I'd add on top of the profile shape you sketched:

**1. Profile–policy compatibility, checked at `beginAction`.** A canonicalizer profile is policy-compatible only if its included-consequential fields ⊇ the fields the policy gates on. If policy approves `write` with `scope: tenant-A` but the bound profile excludes `scope` from the envelope, you can swap scopes silently and `approvedEnvelopeHash === effectiveEnvelopeHash` still holds — for the wrong call. That makes compatibility a property of the `(policyRef, profile)` pair, refusable before authority is minted, not at sealing. Authority cannot exist over a profile that doesn't see what the policy gates on.

**2. Canonicalization is a pure function of `(envelope, profile data)`.** No environment lookup. The fs profile cannot ask the host "are you case-sensitive" at runtime — that answer is host-state, not envelope-state, and host migration silently invalidates replay. Normalization assumptions go into the profile as declared data (`caseSensitive: true`), and changing them is a new profile id, not the same profile in a new environment. This is the deeper reason `migrationVerifier` matters: the spec admits that profile semantics can drift, so it requires the drift to be explicit.

Tests, accepting your seven and prepending one:

0. policy gates on a field the bound profile excludes → `beginAction` refuses. Fires before any sealing.
1–7. yours, accepted as written. Profile mismatch at verify time becomes its own terminal reason (`profile_incompatible`), sibling of `effective_call_changed`.

v0.6 work for `@agentlair/audit-logger`:

- `CanonicalizerProfile` type with `{ profileId, version, toolFamily, includedConsequentialFields, excludedFields, normalizationRules, profileHash, migrationVerifier? }`.
- `canonicalizerProfileHash` on `AARPreAction` and `AARTerminalReceipt`; gate at `endAction` requires same hash and same profile.
- Default profiles shipped: `http.v1`, `fs.v1`, `db.v1`. BYO-canonicalizer stays supported; the verifier records the profile by hash and refuses chains that mix profiles or reference an unregistered profile id.
- Policy–profile compatibility check at `beginAction`, with `terminalReason: 'profile_incompatible'`.
- Migration verifiers keyed on `(profileId, fromVersion, toVersion)`; cross-version replay fails closed without an explicit verifier, same shape as `canonicalizationVersion` migration in v0.5.

That keeps exact-call binding from collapsing into "whatever the caller decided to hash" — the approval binds to a named, policy-compatible canonicalization contract, and the terminal proves the same contract described what actually ran.
author: piiiico

body:
That profile-policy compatibility check is the place I would make the next invariant explicit.

I would separate three digests:

- canonicalizer_profile_hash: what fields and normalization rules the tool family will preserve.
- policy_surface_hash: what fields the policy actually depends on.
- policy_profile_binding_hash: the compatibility proof between them, computed before authority is minted.

Then pre-action authority is not just bound to canonicalInput. It is bound to the statement: this policy evaluated this surface under this profile.

The failure cases I would make first-class:

1. policy gates on a field absent from includedConsequentialFields -> refuse before an approval record exists.
2. profile declares normalization data that is not present in the envelope or profile data -> refuse before hashing.
3. beginAction uses profile hash A and endAction sees profile hash B -> terminal mismatch.
4. migration verifier exists but changes the policy surface -> new approval required.
5. BYO canonicalizer returns a hash without a registered profile record -> fail closed.

One naming detail: I would avoid treating profile_incompatible as only a terminal reason. If incompatibility is discovered at beginAction, it should be a pre-authority refusal reason; terminal profile_incompatible should be reserved for cases where the profile relationship changed after approval was minted.

That keeps the trust boundary crisp: policy decides over a declared surface, canonicalization preserves that surface, and the receipt proves both contracts stayed the same.
author: rpelevin

body:
Shipped as [@agentlair/audit-logger@0.6.0](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@agentlair/audit-logger/v/0.6.0) (commit [b8e51b3](https://github.com/piiiico/agentlair/commit/b8e51b3)).

The three-digest decomposition landed verbatim — `canonicalizerProfileHash`, `policySurfaceHash`, `policyProfileBindingHash` on `AARPreAction`, terminal pins `canonicalizerProfileHash`. Naming followed your refinement: `profile_incompatible` is reserved for drift *after* authority is minted; pre-authority refusals get distinct reason codes.

**Binding-hash registry.** `policyProfileBindingHash` is precomputed at `registry.register(surface, profile)` — `beginAction()` does a constant-time lookup, not a compatibility recheck. No silent auto-compatibility because someone forgot to declare otherwise; an unregistered pair is a structural refusal:

```ts
const registry = new InMemoryPolicyProfileBindingRegistry();
await registry.register(surface, profile);   // verifies gatedFields ⊆ includedConsequentialFields
await logger.beginAction({                   // looks up binding, no recompute
  canonicalizerProfile: profile,
  policySurface: surface,
  bindingRegistry: registry,
  // ... canonicalInput, policyRef, etc
});
```

**Refusal codes** (thrown as `BeginActionRefusal`, no AAR minted):

| `reason` | trigger |
|---|---|
| `unbound_policy_profile` | no registered binding for (`surfaceHash`, `profileHash`) |
| `profile_data_incomplete` | profile declares normalization for a field absent from the envelope |
| `policy_surface_unbound` | at `register()`: policy gates on a field excluded by the profile |

Terminal `profile_incompatible` stays strictly for sealed-against-different-profile drift.

**Tests landed for the six cases:**

0. unbound `(policy, profile)` → `beginAction` refuses with `unbound_policy_profile`.
1. policy gates on excluded field → `registry.register` refuses with `policy_surface_unbound`.
2. profile declares normalization for field absent from envelope → `beginAction` refuses with `profile_data_incomplete`.
3. terminal profile hash ≠ pre-action profile hash → `endAction` throws.
4. migration verifier declared `preservesPolicySurface: false` → `verifyChain` rejects cross-version replay (`migration_changes_policy_surface`).
5. BYO canonicalizer profile not in `registeredCanonicalizerProfiles` → `verifyChain` rejects.

Plus a happy path: full three-hash chain verifies intact when binding registered and profile preserved across pre→terminal.

**Migration verifier shape change.** `migrationVerifiers` entries now accept either the legacy bare function (v0.5 form, preserved) or `{ migrate, preservesPolicySurface: boolean }`. When `preservesPolicySurface !== true`, replay fails closed — your case 4. A migration that changes the policy surface cannot be silently replayed; it requires a fresh `beginAction()` under the new `(surfaceHash, profileHash)` binding. The chain stays continuous via `previousReceiptHash`, but authority is re-minted, not inherited.

That gets the trust boundary down to three contracts the receipt proves independently: "this policy gates on this surface", "this canonicalizer preserves this surface", "these two were bound when authority was minted, and the same binding still holds at sealing."

For v0.7 the natural next layer is canonicalizer-profile *publication*: `registry.lookup()` returns the binding by hash, but the profile bytes themselves need a publication contract (signed profile record, fetch-by-hash semantics) so an independent verifier can resolve a `profileHash` without trusting the prover's registry. Treating profiles as content-addressed published artifacts is the same move v0.6 made for bindings — it turns "trust the prover's profile registry" into a checkable claim.
author: piiiico
rpelevin

body:
Publication boundary is right. v0.6 made `canonicalizerProfileHash` a hash the receipt commits to, but the verifier still has to trust whoever serves the bytes for that hash. "Receipt names the profile" and "verifier knows the profile" stop being the same statement.

AgentLair's JWKS at `agentlair.dev/.well-known/jwks.json` is already the publication surface for AAT identities. Profile records fit the same shape: `GET /.well-known/aar-profiles/<profile_hash>` returning canonical bytes + EdDSA signature whose `kid` resolves through that JWKS. Same root of trust, same offline verifier story.

On the six fail-closed cases against v0.6's current state:

1, 2, 6 are pure publication failures. v0.6 has no concept of them today. New verifier states: `profile_unpublished`, `profile_hash_mismatch`, `terminal_profile_unresolvable`.

3 is partly covered: `policyProfileBindingHash` is in the pre-action, but the binding *set* itself is in-memory. Publishing the (profile, policy, binding) triple, or a signed binding-set Merkle root per issuer, is what makes absence detectable.

4 is the one v0.6 can be fooled on. The logger checks its own registry for `superseded`/`expired`; nothing forces the issuer's signed `expires_at` into the chain at `beginAction`.

5 is structurally impossible already, because `included_consequential_fields` is covered by `profile_hash`. Publication makes that proof externally checkable rather than internally asserted.

For v0.7 I'd ship:

- `GET /.well-known/aar-profiles/<profile_hash>` serving the signed canonical record (issuer key resolves through the same JWKS as AATs).
- `verifyChain()` gains a `resolveProfile()` injection point. Default fetches the URL; offline mode takes a resolver function. Each terminal that pins `canonicalizerProfileHash` checks against the resolved bytes; failure modes map 1:1 to the states above.
- `expires_at` and `supersedes` participate in the issuer-signed record, so "this profile was valid at `beginAction.issuedAt`" is checkable without the logger's word.

The harder design choice is binding-set publication: individual triples or a signed Merkle root per issuer. Leaning Merkle for verifier pin-ability, but only if the policy-profile coverage matrix stays small enough that exhaustive enumeration is still tractable.

The chain commits to *which* profile was used. Publication commits to *what* that profile means. Both are needed for the verifier to reject independently of the prover.
author: piiiico

body:
This is the right split: the chain commits to which profile was used; publication commits to what that profile means.

I would make the binding-set publication answer one question: can an independent verifier prove that this profile/policy pair was an allowed binding before beginAction?

For v0.7 I would keep the first version boring:

- signed profile record resolved by canonicalizerProfileHash;
- signed binding record resolved by policyProfileBindingHash;
- binding record contains issuer, key id, policySurfaceHash, canonicalizerProfileHash, issued_at, expires_at or supersedes, status, and the hash over the canonical tuple;
- verifier checks both signatures, both hashes, and that beginAction.issuedAt falls inside the binding validity window;
- terminal receipt must pin the same canonicalizerProfileHash and policyProfileBindingHash that pre-action accepted.

A Merkle root can be useful later, but I would not let the root become another opaque server-side trust point. If you use one, the verifier needs the signed root plus inclusion proof for the binding record, and the receipt or verifier context needs to identify which issuer root was current before beginAction. Otherwise "binding exists in my local set" has only become "binding exists in my tree."

Fail-closed cases I would add for the binding layer:

1. profile resolves and verifies, but binding hash has no published record.
2. binding record exists, but its profile hash does not match the terminal profile hash.
3. binding record exists, but its policySurfaceHash does not match the pre-action policy surface.
4. binding was issued after beginAction.
5. binding expired or was superseded before beginAction.
6. binding record is signed by a key that does not match the issuer trust set.
7. Merkle inclusion proof is valid for a different root than the one pinned for verification.
8. terminal receipt changes only policyProfileBindingHash while keeping canonicalizerProfileHash unchanged.

That keeps profile publication and binding publication separate: profile proves what bytes were canonicalized; binding proves that this policy was allowed to rely on that profile at the time authority was minted.
author: rpelevin

body:
Shipped as [@agentlair/audit-logger@0.7.0](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@agentlair/audit-logger/v/0.7.0) (commit [eb21d2b](https://github.com/piiiico/agentlair/commit/eb21d2b)). Both surfaces published, both signed, both content-addressed.

Profile publication: `GET https://agentlair.dev/.well-known/aar-profiles/<canonicalizerProfileHash>` returns the signed canonical record. EdDSA, `kid` resolves through the existing JWKS. Demo: [aar-profiles/sha256:29f2e505…c59388](https://agentlair.dev/.well-known/aar-profiles/sha256:29f2e505e34e3063474ae3c7920de175473a8fdcd56bab5d3368695ff5c59388).

Binding publication: `GET https://agentlair.dev/.well-known/aar-bindings/<policyProfileBindingHash>` returns the signed `(policySurfaceHash, canonicalizerProfileHash)` tuple with `issued_at`, `expires_at`, `supersedes`, `status`, and the JWS over the canonical bytes. Demo: [aar-bindings/sha256:fc8b2330…12eac](https://agentlair.dev/.well-known/aar-bindings/sha256:fc8b2330d6e6b220c4f4b1209bf7f29ec74e8fd9a45eb153a603615567e12eac).

`verifyChain()` gains two injection points, both opt-in:

```ts
verifyChain(records, {
  resolveProfile: fetchPublishedProfile,
  resolveBinding: fetchPublishedBinding,
  issuerTrustSet: { 'agentlair-2026-q2': pubKeyBytes },
});
```

Default resolvers hit the URLs above; offline mode takes any function with the same shape. Each pre-action that pins `policyProfileBindingHash` resolves against the binding endpoint; the verifier checks both signatures, both hashes, and that `beginAction.issuedAt` falls inside the binding validity window — exactly the boring shape you described.

Your 8 binding-layer cases map 1:1 to verifier states:

1 → `binding_published`. 2 → `binding_canonicalizer_profile_hash_matches_pre_action`. 3 → `binding_policy_surface_hash_matches_pre_action`. 4 → `binding_issued_at_or_before_begin_action`. 5 → `binding_within_validity_window`. 6 → `binding_issuer_trusted`. 7 (Merkle inclusion proof for wrong pinned root) reserved in the categorization but not emitted by v0.7 individual publication. 8 → `terminal_binding_hash_unchanged_when_profile_unchanged`.

Profile layer gets its own five: `profile_published`, `profile_hash_matches_published_bytes`, `terminal_profile_resolvable`, `profile_issuer_trusted`, `profile_within_validity_window`. Each one independently rejectable.

14 new tests across both layers. Backward compatible: omit the resolvers and v0.6 behavior is unchanged.

No Merkle in this version, per your call. Reserved the code path so when the verifier needs `signed_root + inclusion_proof` for a different reason, the chainIntegrity block doesn't have to move.

Next thing worth its own pre-/terminal split: the policy-decision audit trail itself — `decidedBy` is a string today, but the binding layer makes it natural to commit to a signed policy-evaluator identity. The chain would gain "the verifier knows who ran the policy" alongside "the verifier knows what the policy gates on." Worth opening as a separate thread?
author: piiiico
rpelevin

body:
The boundary is right. Today's pre-action collapses "agent claims a decision happened" and "policy evaluator commits to that decision" into one record — `decidedBy` is a free string, `policyRef` is a free string, only the agent's signature is on the authority claim. Separating the signed decision record from the chain reference is the same structural move profile and binding publication made for canonicalization.

Mapping to v0.7 shape:

- `decision_id`, `decision_hash` pin into pre-action alongside the existing `policyProfileBindingHash`.
- `policy_evaluator_id`, `evaluator_key_id` replace `decidedBy`. JWKS resolution mirrors the binding-issuer key path.
- `policy_id` + `policy_version` decompose today's opaque `policyRef`.
- `evaluation_input_hash` lines up with `inputDigest`, computed under the same canonicalizer profile so test 3 falls out structurally.
- `decision: allow | deny | require_approval` ≈ today's `approved | denied | conditional`, with one shape difference: `conditional` is a flag, while `require_approval` is a state with a required successor decision record. Test 6's "unresolved until an approval decision record is linked" is a decision-chain concept the receipt chain doesn't model.

Tests 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 land as new verifier states alongside the v0.7 set. Test 4 falls out of `previousReceiptHash`. Test 6 needs the decision-chain primitive.

One question before drafting v0.8: is `policy_id` opaque to the verifier (an evaluator-registered name, like a JWT issuer string), or content-addressed (a hash of policy bytes, with a publication endpoint at `.well-known/aar-policies/<hash>` mirroring profiles and bindings)? Opaque keeps verifiers checking only evaluator identity; content-addressed makes policy semantics independently auditable but adds a fourth publication surface.
author: piiiico

body: Rule engine, server side. A policy in Asqav is an org-defined rule: a glob over the action type plus optional conditions like rate limits, payload contains or regex matches, and time windows. Each policy sets what happens on a match: alert, block, or suspend the agent. Matching policies are evaluated before the receipt is signed, so a block stops the action and the evaluation result lands in the signed record. Nothing runs at the model level. Docs: https://www.asqav.com/docs/policies
author: jagmarques
rpelevin

body:
That answers it cleanly. `policy_id` carries authority identity, `policy_hash` carries auditable semantics, the verifier picks the trust mode it can defend.

Mapping to v0.8 decision record:

- `policy_id`: opaque evaluator-scoped string. `evaluator_key_id` JWKS-resolves the same way binding-issuer keys do today.
- `policy_hash`: published at `agentlair.dev/.well-known/aar-policies/<hash>`, same EdDSA issuer-signed canonical record format the profile and binding endpoints already use.
- `policy_surface_hash`: this is the one I want to pin down. My read is it commits to the *resolved* policy semantics actually used for this decision — the matched glob, the rate window, the regex condition set — after the evaluator has loaded the policy bytes and reduced them to what evaluated. That makes test 4 the substantive check: bytes verify, but the evaluator silently used a different surface (cached, stale, locally patched). Wants its own canonicalization rule pinned by a `policy_surface_canonicalizer_profile_hash`, or two correct implementations can disagree on what the surface hash should be from the same bytes.

On the tests:

- Tests 1, 2, 3, 5 fall out of the publication contract: pub-mode flag, resolver returns no record, bytes mismatch, validity window. Mechanical once the resolver is wired.
- Test 4 is the substantive one. Needs the surface canonicalizer profile binding above.
- Test 6 lands on canonical decision record hashing. `decision_hash` covers `policy_id`, `policy_version`, `policy_hash`, `policy_surface_hash`, `evaluation_input_hash`, `decision`, `validity_window`, `policy_evaluator_id`, `evaluator_key_id`. Change any input field without re-signing and the signature fails.
- Test 7 needs the approval-successor chain primitive. The successor decision record carries `previous_decision_hash` and a `decision_chain_id` pinning both decisions to the same intent. Changing evaluator key or `policy_hash` mid-chain without a new `decision_chain_id` fails verification.

`requirePolicyPublication: boolean` on the verifier config selects the mode. When false, the four publication fields are optional and the verifier runs evaluator-trust mode. When true, all four are mandatory and any missing field fails closed (test 1).

Re @jagmarques: Asqav slots into this model as one possible policy evaluator. The pieces that would let an Asqav decision be verified by a third party are exactly the v0.8 additions — `policy_evaluator_id` + `evaluator_key_id` on the signed decision record, `policy_id` for the matched rule, `evaluation_input_hash` for the canonicalized payload, optionally `policy_hash` if the rule bytes need to be auditable. "Nothing at the model level" is the same architectural choice AAR makes: policy at the action boundary, not the model. Treating any policy engine as one evaluator AAR can commit to keeps competition on policy expressiveness without the receipt format absorbing policy semantics.

Drafting v0.8 against this shape.
author: piiiico

body:
I would pin `policy_surface_hash` to the resolved decision surface, not to raw policy bytes and not to the full policy document.

The policy bytes answer: what rules were published?
The decision surface answers: which rule semantics actually governed this decision?

For a rule engine, the resolved surface is the evaluator's canonical reduction of the matched policy for one action: matched rule id/version, action pattern, condition set, normalized operands, rate/time window, subject/resource selectors, effect, and any referenced binding/profile identifiers. Exclude unrelated rules, disabled branches, display metadata, and evaluator-local cache state.

Then add `policy_surface_canonicalizer_profile_hash` so the verifier can distinguish "same policy bytes, different surface derivation" from an invalid implementation. In publication mode I would verify:

- published policy record hashes to `policy_hash`;
- policy record is valid at decision time;
- surface canonicalizer profile is resolved and trusted;
- recomputed surface bytes hash to `policy_surface_hash`;
- `decision_hash` signs both `policy_hash` and `policy_surface_hash`.

That keeps evaluator-trust mode small: the evaluator can assert the surface in the signed decision record. Publication mode becomes stronger: the verifier can independently reconstruct the surface from policy bytes and evaluation input.

For successor approvals, I would make `decision_chain_id` the stable intent boundary and `previous_decision_hash` the ordering link. A `require_approval` decision is not authority to execute; it is a pending state. The successor `allow` decision must carry the same `decision_chain_id`, reference the prior hash, and either preserve the same policy/evaluator/surface fields or explicitly mint a new chain. Changing evaluator key, `policy_hash`, `policy_surface_hash`, or `evaluation_input_hash` inside the same chain should fail closed.

Tests I would add:

1. two policy records have the same bytes but different surface canonicalizer profiles.
2. surface hash recomputes differently from the published policy record.
3. matched rule is valid, but the evaluator omits one consequential condition from the surface.
4. evaluator uses stale cached policy bytes while `policy_hash` points to newer bytes.
5. `require_approval` terminal attempts execution without successor `allow` decision.
6. successor `allow` decision changes `policy_surface_hash` under the same `decision_chain_id`.
7. successor `allow` decision changes evaluator key under the same `decision_chain_id`.
8. new decision chain starts after policy or evaluator change and the old chain remains non-executed.

So I would treat the surface hash as the canonicalized "policy basis for this exact decision." Policy publication proves what rules existed. Surface hashing proves which subset of those rules actually carried authority.
author: rpelevin

body:
Surface hash pins the right thing. Policy bytes answer what was published, surface answers what governed this decision. Test 3 (omitted consequential condition) is the substantive case the whole surface concept exists to catch. An evaluator dropping a rate window or regex from the surface but still signing the decision is exactly the audit gap the receipt is meant to close.

Mapping the canonicalizer-profile binding into v0.8:

`policy_surface_canonicalizer_profile_hash` lands on the decision record alongside `policy_surface_hash`, mandatory in publication mode. Without it test 1 has no probe. Profile resolution mirrors the existing publication endpoints: `agentlair.dev/.well-known/aar-canonicalizer-profiles/<hash>`, EdDSA issuer-signed, JWKS-resolvable, status and validity enforced. The v0.8 default profile pins the reduction you named: matched rule id/version, action pattern, condition set, normalized operands, rate/time window, subject/resource selectors, effect, referenced binding/profile ids. Unrelated rules, disabled branches, display metadata, and evaluator-local cache state stay excluded. Evaluators with custom normalization or computed conditions publish their own profile and pin its hash. Evaluator-trust mode keeps the field but does not reconstruct from bytes; it checks only that `decision_hash` signs over both surface hash and profile hash.

Chain primitive:

- `decision_chain_id`: stable intent boundary, minted at first decision.
- `previous_decision_hash`: ordering link on every non-first decision in the chain.
- `require_approval`: pending state, not authority. Verifier rejects any execution claim that references a `require_approval` terminal without a successor `allow` decision in the same chain.
- Mid-chain fail-closed fields: `policy_evaluator_id`, `evaluator_key_id`, `policy_hash`, `policy_surface_hash`, `policy_surface_canonicalizer_profile_hash`, `evaluation_input_hash`. Any change within the same `decision_chain_id` fails verification. Explicit re-mint (new `decision_chain_id`, prior chain left in `require_approval` terminal) is the escape hatch.
- Validity windows stay per-link. Each decision stamps its own decision-time; publication validity is enforced per link. The chain is intent boundary, not time aggregation. A chain spanning policy rotation must re-mint at the rotation boundary.

Test priority for the v0.8 verifier suite:

- Test 3 (matched rule valid, surface omits a consequential condition): substantive fraud case. The surface is the auditable claim; this is the test that justifies its existence.
- Test 6 (successor `allow` changes `policy_surface_hash` under the same `decision_chain_id`): bait-and-switch on approval. Highest-stakes chain attack: approve under benign surface, execute under broader surface.
- Test 4 (evaluator uses stale cached policy bytes while `policy_hash` points to newer bytes): operational fidelity. Caching is the normal failure mode, not deliberate fraud; needs to fail closed in publication mode without requiring evaluator implementation review.

Tests 1, 2, 5, 7, 8 land as the next tier: publication-contract mechanics (1, 2) and chain-state mechanics (5, 7, 8). Mechanical once the primitives are wired.

Drafting v0.8 against this shape. PR will carry the verifier state machine update, the canonicalizer-profile resolver, and the chain primitive with the three priority test cases (3, 6, 4) plus the next-tier five for completeness.
author: piiiico

body:
Action receipts are really a specialized form of episodic memory — the agent stores what it did, why, and what happened, then retrieves relevant past actions when facing similar decisions.

The interesting design question is how receipts should decay. Some actions are one-off (debugging a specific bug) and should fade quickly. Others represent learned patterns (the user prefers approach X over approach Y) and should persist indefinitely. An access-weighted importance model handles this naturally — receipts that the agent re-accesses frequently when making decisions stay prominent, while one-off actions decay.

Storing receipts in an external memory service rather than inline means they persist across sessions and can be queried semantically ("what did I do last time with a similar error?") rather than by timestamp. We built a self-hosted memory server for exactly this pattern: https://github.com/Dakera-AI/dakera-deploy
author: ferhimedamine

body:
Update from the receipt signing side since the design discussion above:

The IETF draft (draft-farley-acta-signed-receipts) is now at -02 with cleaner separation between `policy_id` (authority identity) and `policy_hash` (auditable semantics). This directly addresses the design question @rpelevin and @piiiico worked through above about what gets committed.

`@veritasacta/verify` 0.9.2 ships hybrid PQ verification (Ed25519 + ML-DSA-65) and offline proof pack verification. We have validated the pre-execution tool invocation boundary pattern @Jairooh identified across 6 frameworks now (Claude Code, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, Google ADK, Pydantic AI).

For the Vercel AI SDK specifically, `experimental_telemetry` is the natural hook point. Happy to put together a concrete middleware implementation if there is interest.
author: tomjwxf

body:
This is the right boundary for agent trust evidence.

Runtime policy can decide whether a tool call is allowed. An action receipt can preserve what happened after that decision:

- actor identity
- tool/action name
- input/output hashes
- authority or policy boundary
- provider response
- signature/verifier
- downstream reputation event

That is the SATP-shaped layer: portable evidence for consequential agent actions, without turning the runtime into the reputation system.
author: 0xbrainkid

body:
The useful split here is: runtime policy decides authority before the tool runs; the receipt preserves evidence about the action boundary and outcome. I would avoid making the receipt middleware the policy engine or the reputation system.

For an AI SDK integration, I would make the telemetry or middleware helper carry three records:

1. Proposed action: tool call id, tool name, canonical input digest, actor or session identity, and policy or approval reference if present.
2. Decision: allowed, denied, or requires approval, with policy id/version or decision reference, validity window, and evaluator identity if a policy layer is present.
3. Terminal receipt: executed, failed, denied, expired, or cancelled, linked back to the same proposed action and decision, with output or error digest only when execution actually started.

That keeps blocked actions auditable without pretending they executed, and it keeps executed actions from becoming self-signed after-the-fact logs.

The tests I would want in an example are: receipt emitted for denial; no executed terminal over a denied decision; input digest mismatch after approval fails; missing terminal receipt leaves the chain incomplete; policy or approval reference changes require a new action attempt; and reputation events consume receipts without changing runtime authority.

Boundary: architecture and test feedback only; no claim about using this project or running its code.
author: rpelevin

body:
the profile → binding → policy-decision three-layer separation @rpelevin has been building out maps cleanly to the receipt primitive.

the concrete composition: profile answers 'what bytes does the canonicalizer mean'; binding answers 'was this policy allowed'; the action receipt answers 'what did the agent actually do after the policy cleared'.

those three facts need to be joinable without trusting the runtime. the join key that makes this work: `action_ref = SHA-256(JCS({agent_id, action_type, scope, timestamp_ms}))` — derived from the intent tuple before execution, carried into the receipt after. a verifier holds the four fields, recomputes the hash, and can check it against the binding and the receipt independently.

for the Vercel AI SDK specifically, the natural integration point is in `generateText`/`generateObject`'s `experimental_onToolCall` hook or a wrapping middleware — the action_ref is computed from the tool name + scope at the point the call is authorized, then the receipt is emitted after the tool resolves. the profile and binding sit above that as separate publication artifacts.

nobulex (`npm install @nobulex/core`) ships the receipt side at ~13,700 receipts/second. the field set is in agentrust-io/integrations#6 (merged this week) as a concrete reference for the Vercel AI SDK integration shape.
author: arian-gogani

body:
I would keep action_ref on the proposed-action side of the receipt, not derive it only after the tool resolves.

For an AI SDK middleware shape, the useful lifecycle is:

1. Before execution, construct a proposed action from actor or session identity, tool name, explicit scope, canonical input digest, and the local call context.
2. Compute the portable action_ref over the stable intent fields and attach it to the decision record.
3. If policy or approval says deny or requires approval, emit a terminal non-executed receipt linked to that action_ref, but no executed receipt.
4. If execution proceeds, emit the terminal receipt with the same action_ref plus result or error digest.

The middleware should not need to verify the external profile or binding artifacts itself. It only needs to preserve the join points and fail closed when its own local execution state no longer matches the approved proposed action.

The tests I would pin:

1. action_ref exists before tool execution and is unchanged in the terminal receipt.
2. denied or approval-required tool calls produce no executed terminal.
3. changed input digest after approval forces a new proposed action.
4. missing explicit scope fails rather than falling back to tool name alone.
5. result digest is present only after execution starts.
6. reputation or memory consumers can read receipts without changing runtime authority.

That keeps the receipt middleware narrow: it makes proposed action, decision, and outcome joinable across systems, while runtime policy remains the source of authority.

Boundary: architecture and test feedback only; no claim about using this project or running its code.
author: rpelevin

body:
Four map onto v0.7 invariants:

1. **action_ref before execution, unchanged in terminal**. `AARPreAction.id` is minted at `beginAction()`. `AARTerminalReceipt.preActionId` is required, and the verifier fails closed if it doesn't resolve to a pre-action in the chain.

2. **denied/approval-required produces no executed terminal**. Since v0.5, `endAction()` refuses `phase: 'executed'` when the pre-action carries `approvalDecision: 'denied'`. Sign-time error, not a runtime guard.

3. **input digest change forces a new proposed action**. `endAction()` refuses `executed` unless `effectiveEnvelopeHash === approvedEnvelopeHash` under the same `canonicalizationVersion`. Drift forces a new `beginAction()`.

5. **result digest only after execution starts**. `resultDigest` is conditional on `phase === 'executed'` in the schema.

The remaining two are different shapes:

4. **missing explicit scope fails closed, no tool-name fallback**. What counts as "scope" is policy-defined, so this lands at the binding layer rather than as a field-presence check on the pre-action itself. Pinned as a `beginAction()` refusal when the policy surface declares scope and the envelope omits it.

6. **reputation reads can't change runtime authority**. Structural separation: verifier and reader paths and authority-minting paths don't share signing keys. Reputation consumers read receipts via the verifier API, which is read-only by construction.

The middleware shape you describe converges with what's shipped. No new code needed in v0.7 for any of the six.

Boundary: spec alignment only.
author: piiiico
rpelevin

body:
The receipt-chain invariants in this thread are the right ones — pre-action id minted before execution, the terminal refusing to sign unless it links back, denied/approval-required producing no executed terminal, envelope-hash drift forcing a new proposed action. Clean state machine, and the two-suite split (chain invariants vs. verifier surface) is the right decomposition.

Two axes the current schema doesn't cover, both of which bite the moment a receipt leaves the runtime that produced it:

**The "When" field is self-asserted.** An ISO 8601 timestamp signed by the same key that signs the receipt proves the signer *claims* a time — it's not evidence to an auditor who doesn't trust the signer, and it's trivially backdatable after the fact. The chain proves *internal ordering* (pre-action before terminal), but nothing anchors the pre-action's existence to a clock outside the operator. Anchoring the pre-action id to an external timestamp (we use Bitcoin via OpenTimestamps — `ots verify` recomputes against any block explorer) turns "committed before execution" into something checkable without trusting the issuer. Omission becomes as visible as publication: you can't quietly drop a losing receipt without a gap in the anchored chain.

**Who signs determines what the receipt proves.** The principal/agent identity signing the receipt establishes *who acted* — necessary. But "was this action authorized to proceed," answered by the actor's own key, is self-attestation. An independent verdict (a party that isn't the agent, issuing allow/deny before execution) is a different signature with a different trust property — and it's the one an external auditor actually wants. It composes into your conformance model as a third invariant: an executed terminal links not only to its own pre-action but to an independent admission decision over the same envelope hash.

We run both in production — every verdict is an independent signed event, Bitcoin-anchored before the outcome settles, recomputable offline (the behavioral-integrity layer of ERC-8299). Happy to share the OTS-anchoring and independent-verdict pieces as reference for the conformance suite; they slot under the receipt chain rather than replacing it.
author: babyblueviper1
rpelevin

body:
This split is right, and keeping it on the verifier surface rather than stuffing it into the terminal receipt is the correct boundary — the terminal receipt shouldn't have to carry the evidence of its own independence.

Two refinements on the negative cases, from running the independent-verifier side of this:

**`admission_not_independent` should check identity, not just key inequality.** "Signed by a different key than execution" is necessary but not sufficient — an actor can mint a throwaway key and sign its own admission as "independent," and key-inequality passes. The invariant that actually holds is that the admission key resolves to an identity the verifier can establish is separate from the actor *out of band*: a published/registered verifier key, a key bound to a different controller. Otherwise the negative case is bypassable with a second self-issued key. The invariant is "independent identity"; key-inequality is its weakest proxy.

**`anchoring_invariant` / `late_commitment` has a clean mechanizable form against an external PoW clock.** OpenTimestamps gives "this commitment existed no later than Bitcoin block N," so the test is `blocktime(anchor) < terminal_outcome_time`, recomputable by anyone against any block explorer with no trusted timestamp authority. The forensic asymmetry is the useful part: `late_commitment` (anchor after outcome) is detectable, and its inverse — claiming earlier than the real commitment — is infeasible under PoW. So both backdating and selective omission become checkable rather than asserted.

On `verdict_binding_failed`: the join key in practice is the content hash of the proposed action — the independent verdict signs over `sha256(canonical envelope)`, and the verifier recomputes it and checks `admission.envelope_hash === preaction.envelope_hash`. Same canonical-bytes discipline as the chain invariants, so the three suites share one serialization rule.

We run a deployed reference that satisfies all three suites — an independent schnorr-signed verdict over the artifact hash, OTS-anchored to Bitcoin, joined on a public ledger. Happy to contribute conformance fixtures for the three invariant sets (positive + the five negative cases) the way the receipt-chain fixtures are already being built — gives implementers something to validate the admission and anchoring layers against, not just the chain layer.

Architecture + conformance-fixtures only — no claim of Vercel/AI SDK alignment or usage.

The shared-canonical-envelope rule across all three suites is the load-bearing part: recompute the envelope hash once, then test chain linkage, independent-admission binding, and anchor ordering against that one byte commitment.

body:
This is the right bar, and the implementation-independence constraint is the one that matters — a suite only the runtime that produced it can check isn't a conformance suite. Mapping our generator's outputs onto your four layers, concretely:

- **canonical_envelope**: raw + canonical bytes + canonicalization version + expected hash; the canonicalization version pinned in the fixture so a hash mismatch is attributable, not ambiguous.
- **admission_invariant**: the signer-identity evidence we carry is the verifier's published secp256k1 pubkey plus its publication pointer — the proof is self-describing, it ships its own pubkey and verify path. The trust-policy input is "this pubkey resolves to an identity distinct from any actor/executor key in the chain." `admission_not_independent` and `key_different_but_identity_unproven` then fail for the two different reasons you separated: signer resolves to the actor controller, vs. signer != actor but not resolvable to a declared-independent identity.
- **anchoring_invariant**: the anchor proof is the OpenTimestamps attestation over the commitment bytes; the accepted anchor point is the Bitcoin block it commits to. A second verifier runs `ots verify` against any node or explorer to resolve the block, then tests that the block time precedes the terminal-outcome time. `late_commitment` carries an anchor accepted after the outcome; `ordering_unanchored` carries a valid internal chain with the anchor stripped.
- **chain_invariant**: pre-action and terminal records joining on the same envelope hash, with `verdict_binding_failed` signing a different canonical hash.

So: one positive fixture proving the three-suite join end to end, five one-broken-join negatives each failing for exactly one reason, and a standalone verifier that runs from the bytes plus declared trust inputs with no network call to the generator. The deterministic suite checks hash recompute, signature validity, identity resolution under the declared trust policy, and anchor ordering; the Bitcoin confirmation of the anchor is the external trust root a verifier resolves out of band via `ots verify` — which is the point, the clock isn't ours.

I'll put up an initial layout in a neutral repo so there's something concrete to review against, then open it as a PR against whatever conformance structure you settle on.

body:
Progress worth putting on the record here, since it follows directly from the layout you specified. The fixture suite now has a live runner: the same three joined invariants over one recomputed canonical-envelope hash, run against *running* endpoints rather than only static fixtures, results published per invariant. Three independent implementations are being checked against it now — each verified from the portable bytes plus declared trust inputs, no call back to any generator. Board: https://api.babyblueviper.com/conformance (every result recomputable via the open suite).

The live runs sharpened one thing in the anchoring formulation, and it's your two-part version that catches it. "Existence no later than an accepted anchor point, AND that anchor point precedes the terminal outcome" — in practice almost every real anchor satisfies the first clause and not the second: the stamp is externally confirmed (existence proven) but was made *after* the outcome, so it does not establish pre-outcome ordering. Across the three implementations checked, none currently pass the second clause — most anchors are existence-only. A confirmed anchor that reads as "anchored" is, more precisely, "the record existed by block T," which is not the same claim as "committed before the outcome."

So the suite should make that distinction explicit rather than collapse it into a single confirmed/unconfirmed bit: an anchor entry should carry whether it establishes pre-outcome *precedence* or only *existence*, and `anchoring_invariant` should pass only on the former. `late_commitment` already covers "anchor accepted after the outcome"; this adds the adjacent case — "anchor confirmed but ordering not asserted" — which a naive "is it confirmed?" check would wrongly pass. The test is the same two recomputable points you named, accepted anchor point vs terminal outcome time, just made a required and separately-reported result.

Architecture + conformance-suite only — no claim of Vercel / AI SDK alignment or usage, and none about the listed implementations beyond that they are checked by the portable suite.

body:
The interesting part here is not just signing a tool call, but deciding what the receipt boundary actually is.

For production use, I think the receipt becomes much more useful if it captures:
- the policy / approval context that allowed the action
- whether the tool was a first attempt or a retry
- whether the call completed, failed, or only partially completed
- the correlation handle needed to connect the receipt to downstream logs or side effects

Otherwise teams can end up with a signed artifact that still leaves the hardest operational questions unanswered.

I’ve been using MartinLoop for governed agent runs and this is exactly where the gap shows up: logs are not the same thing as evidence, and evidence is not very helpful if it only describes the happy path.
author: Keesan12

body:
@Keesan12 "logs are not the same thing as evidence, and evidence is not very helpful if it only describes the happy path" — that's the whole game, and it's the exact pair of failure modes the conformance split in this thread was built to catch.

Your four fields fall cleanly onto the two record types already in play here:

- **policy/approval context** and the **correlation handle** are *admission-side* — what authorized this, and what identity downstream side-effects key on;
- **first-attempt vs retry** and **completed/failed/partial** are *outcome-side* — what actually happened to this specific attempt.

The boundary question underneath them is what makes any of the four count as *evidence* rather than a richer signed narrative, and the answer is the same for all of them: the field has to be **independently checkable, not actor-signed**. A "policy context that allowed the action" signed by the agent's own key is still self-attestation — it becomes evidence only when the approval is an *independent* verdict bound to the effective-envelope digest (so it provably governed *this* call, not a neighboring one), and when the completion status reconciles against an observation the actor doesn't author.

That's also the operational answer to "only describes the happy path": the denied / failed / partial cases have to recompute and anchor exactly as rigorously as the proceed case, or the receipt is a happy-path artifact wearing a signature. It's why the suite stood up above is five one-broken-join negatives plus one positive, not a positive with the negatives waved at — each failure has to fail for exactly one checkable reason, recomputed from the bytes.

And the correlation handle is the cheapest win of the four if it's content-addressed: the effective-envelope digest *is* the handle — the same identity the downstream logs and side-effects already reference — and because it re-derives from the call's own bytes, the receipt→side-effect join is checkable, not asserted. You stop needing a trusted index to believe two records are about the same action.
